title: Shoulder-Check Gate Receive
primarySkill: Scanning while moving to receive
objective: Teach players to complete purposeful shoulder checks while moving towards possession so they recognise space and pressure behind them before receiving.
groundSize: 15 × 20 metres per group.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Create a starting cone for the receiver.
Position a ball carrier 12–15 metres in front.
Place two exit gates five metres behind the receiver’s starting position, one to the left and one to the right.
Position one signal player behind the receiver with two coloured markers.
Place one target player beyond each exit gate.
Use parallel lanes for larger groups.
howTheDrillWorks:
The receiver begins facing the ball carrier.
The signal player quietly raises one coloured marker behind the receiver.
The receiver leads towards the ball carrier and completes a shoulder check while moving.
The receiver calls the colour and receives a handball or short kick.
The receiver turns through the gate matching the observed colour.
The player disposes to the target beyond that gate.
Players rotate from ball carrier to receiver, receiver to target, target to signal player and signal player to ball carrier.
Alternate the shoulder from which the information must be collected.
coachingPoints: Check the shoulder early enough to process the information before receiving.
Maintain running rhythm during the scan.
Avoid turning the entire body away from the football.
Return the eyes to the football before the disposal arrives.
Receive with hands prepared and body balanced.
Turn towards the selected gate without stopping.
Use both shoulders depending on the direction of movement.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: The timing of the shoulder check.
Whether players lose speed while scanning.
Whether players scan from both sides.
The cleanliness of the receive after the scan.
Whether the turn begins immediately after possession.
Whether players run through the selected gate rather than drifting sideways.

commonErrors.error: Player stops before scanning.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce the running speed and require continuous movement.

commonErrors.error: Player turns too far and loses sight of the football.
commonErrors.correction: Coach a short chin-to-shoulder check rather than a full-body turn.

commonErrors.error: Player guesses the gate.
commonErrors.correction: Require the colour to be called before the disposal is released.

commonErrors.error: Player receives flat-footed.
commonErrors.correction: Deliver the football slightly in front of the receiver.

commonErrors.error: Player only scans over the preferred shoulder.
commonErrors.correction: Alternate the signal player’s position and prescribed checking side.

progressions: Add a passive defender who approaches from one gate.
Change the cue after the player’s first scan to require a second check.
Increase the disposal distance.
Allow the receiver to choose between a handball and kick after exiting.
Add a trailing player who applies realistic closing pressure.
regressions: Use one fixed exit gate at a time.
Have the signal player call the colour as well as display it.
Shorten the lead and disposal distance.
successIndicators: Complete a visible shoulder check without stopping.
Exit through the correct gate at speed.
matchApplication: Players regularly lead towards the football with opponents, teammates and open space positioned behind or beside them. A controlled shoulder check allows the receiver to know whether to turn, protect the football, release quickly or hold possession.

title: Find the Free Space
primarySkill: Identifying usable space
objective: Develop players’ ability to recognise and move into the most useful available space before receiving possession.
groundSize: 20 × 20 metres divided into four equal zones.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Divide a 20 × 20-metre square into four smaller zones.
Position one receiver in the central area.
Place a teammate on two outside boundaries.
Place two passive blockers inside two of the zones.
One ball carrier begins outside the square.
Blockers may stand in or move slowly through their assigned zones.
howTheDrillWorks:
The receiver scans the four zones before beginning a lead.
The receiver identifies which zone provides the greatest space and clearest path away from the blockers.
The receiver leads into that zone and communicates for the football.
The ball carrier disposes to the receiver’s advantage.
The receiver takes possession and connects with an outside teammate.
The blockers change zones after each repetition.
The receiver must reassess rather than repeating a memorised lead.
Rotate roles after three to four repetitions.
coachingPoints: Scan the whole area rather than focusing on the nearest cone.
Identify both open space and the path required to reach it.
Lead late enough to prevent the space being closed too early.
Accelerate into the chosen zone.
Communicate clearly once the decision has been made.
Deliver the football into the receiver’s path.
Reassess if the preferred space becomes occupied.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the receiver scans before moving.
Whether players recognise the largest useful space.
The timing and speed of the lead.
Whether the disposal supports the receiver’s decision.
Whether the receiver adjusts when a blocker changes position.
Whether players confuse empty space with space that is difficult to access.

commonErrors.error: Receiver runs to the nearest zone without scanning.
commonErrors.correction: Require the player to point to the chosen zone before leading.

commonErrors.error: Receiver leads into space that is already closing.
commonErrors.correction: Encourage a second scan immediately before acceleration.

commonErrors.error: Lead is too early and easily tracked.
commonErrors.correction: Hold the starting position longer and accelerate later.

commonErrors.error: Ball carrier kicks to the receiver rather than into space.
commonErrors.correction: Place a target cone beyond the receiver’s intended path.

commonErrors.error: Receiver changes direction repeatedly without committing.
commonErrors.correction: Set a three-second decision limit.

progressions: Allow blockers to move freely between zones.
Add a defender who tracks the receiver.
Require the ball carrier to choose between multiple receivers.
Add a second disposal after the receive.
Score extra points when the receiver uses the largest available zone.
regressions: Make the blocked zones stationary and obvious.
Allow the coach to call the free zone.
Reduce the area to three zones.
successIndicators: Select space that is both open and accessible.
Accelerate decisively into the chosen area.
matchApplication: The drill replicates leading for possession, spreading from congestion and creating a clear disposal option. Recognising useful space early helps players avoid crowding the football and improves the team’s ability to retain possession.

title: Decision-Making Fundamentals Circuit
primarySkill: Integrated fundamental decision making
objective: Assess and reinforce the fundamental decision-making behaviours introduced in DM-001 to DM-009 through a progressive multi-station circuit.
groundSize: Four stations using approximately half a ground.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Create four stations:
Station 1 – Scan and Receive: Players identify a visual cue before receiving.
Station 2 – Space and Pressure: Players lead into free space and react to a closing defender.
Station 3 – Option and Risk: Players select between safe, attacking and switch options.
Station 4 – Numbers and Field Position: Small-sided play begins with changing numbers and nominated field zones.
Divide the squad evenly between stations. Assign a coach or leader to each station where possible.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete four minutes of work at each station.
Station 1 scores scanning timing, body position and clean possession.
Station 2 scores space recognition and correct response to pressure.
Station 3 scores option selection and risk awareness.
Station 4 scores recognition of numerical advantage and field-position context.
Players receive one point for an appropriate decision and one point for successful execution.
Rotate after four minutes with one minute for explanation and movement.
Complete two circuits if time allows.
In the second circuit, increase pressure or reduce decision time.
Finish with a brief review of the most common team strengths and errors.
coachingPoints: Gather information before possession whenever possible.
Scan space, teammates, opponents and pressure sources.
Make the decision before perfect execution is demanded.
Recognise that the best option changes with field position and numbers.
Take attacking opportunities when the advantage is clear.
Retain possession when the risk is greater than the likely reward.
Re-scan after every disposal and turnover.
Separate decision quality from execution when assessing players.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether scanning occurs before possession.
Whether players identify useful space.
Whether decisions change appropriately under pressure.
Whether players select options that support the next phase.
Whether risk is adjusted to field position.
Whether players recognise numerical advantage.
Whether execution errors occur despite correct decisions.
Whether the same decision errors repeat across multiple stations.

commonErrors.error: Players focus only on completing the skill.
commonErrors.correction: Score decision quality separately from execution quality.

commonErrors.error: Scanning disappears when pressure increases.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce speed briefly and rebuild the pre-possession habit.

commonErrors.error: Players use the same option regardless of the picture.
commonErrors.correction: Change cues, defender positions and numerical situations frequently.

commonErrors.error: Players become overly conservative.
commonErrors.correction: Reward correct attacking decisions even when execution is imperfect.

commonErrors.error: Coaches provide the answer before the player decides.
commonErrors.correction: Use questioning after the action rather than directing during it.

commonErrors.error: Station rotations become disorganised.
commonErrors.correction: Use fixed groups, clear rotation direction and visible station numbers.

progressions: Remove verbal cues and rely on live information.
Increase defensive pressure.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Connect all four stations into one continuous transition activity.
Ask players to self-assess and explain selected decisions.
Record individual decision scores across repeated sessions.
regressions: Run two stations at a time.
Allow a brief pause before possession.
Demonstrate the preferred scanning pattern at each station.
Remove scoring and focus on one decision behaviour per rotation.
successIndicators: Explain why a selected decision was appropriate.
Maintain decision quality as pressure increases.
matchApplication: The circuit brings together the core information-processing demands of Australian football. Players must scan, interpret space and pressure, assess risk, recognise numbers and choose an action that suits the position and phase of play.

title: Call, Point and Confirm
primarySkill: Validating communicated options
objective: Teach players to use teammate communication as useful information while visually confirming that the called option is genuinely available.
groundSize: 18 × 22 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Position one ball carrier in the centre of the area.
Place three target players around the outside.
Set one passive defender between the ball carrier and the targets.
Two targets call for possession during each repetition.
Only one target has a clear passing lane.
Targets must call, point to the intended space and continue moving.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier receives from a feeder.
Two targets immediately call and point to their preferred receiving space.
The passive defender positions to block one of the called options.
The ball carrier scans both the callers and the passing lanes.
The player disposes to the target whose communication is supported by the visual picture.
A point is awarded for selecting the genuinely available option.
The target receiving the football becomes the next ball carrier.
The previous ball carrier moves into a target position.
The defender changes the blocked lane on every repetition.
coachingPoints: Communication provides information but does not make the decision.
Look at the teammate, the defender and the space being indicated.
Calls should be early, specific and connected to movement.
Point to usable space rather than only calling a name.
Do not call when positioned behind a defender.
The ball carrier remains responsible for the final choice.
Continue communicating after the first disposal.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether calls are early and specific.
Whether targets point to realistic receiving space.
Whether the ball carrier visually confirms the lane.
Whether players blindly follow the loudest call.
Whether targets stop moving after communicating.
Whether the defender’s position is recognised.

commonErrors.error: Ball carrier disposes to the loudest player without scanning.
commonErrors.correction: Require the player to identify the defender before releasing the football.

commonErrors.error: Targets call while standing behind the defender.
commonErrors.correction: Coach lateral movement before the call.

commonErrors.error: Players point at themselves rather than into space.
commonErrors.correction: Require the hand signal to show where the disposal should go.

commonErrors.error: Calls occur after the decision has already been made.
commonErrors.correction: Encourage communication before or as possession is received.

commonErrors.error: Ball carrier ignores all communication.
commonErrors.correction: Ask the player to repeat the useful call before disposing.

progressions: Add a second defender.
Allow defenders to intercept.
Introduce one deliberately poor call that must be rejected.
Continue play through three consecutive decisions.
Give the ball carrier a two-second disposal limit.
regressions: Use two targets and one blocked option.
Allow the coach to demonstrate useful calls.
successIndicators: Communicate before the ball carrier is under pressure.
Select and execute the best available disposal.
matchApplication: Players depend on teammates for pressure calls, switches, short options and forward leads. This drill reinforces that communication assists awareness, but the player in possession must still verify the option against the live defensive picture.

title: Take, Tap or Soccer
primarySkill: Ground-ball action selection
objective: Teach players to decide whether to take clean possession, tap the football to a teammate or soccer it forward according to pressure, support and field position.
groundSize: 18 × 25 metres with a scoring gate at one end.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Roll or bounce the football into a central contest area.
Position one approaching attacker, one supporting teammate and one defender.
Set a target teammate to the side and a scoring gate ahead.
Vary the defender’s starting distance and angle.
The support player may be close enough for a tap or too far away to assist.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach rolls the football into the area.
The attacker scans the defender, support player and space ahead while approaching.
With time and balance, the attacker takes clean possession.
Under immediate pressure with a clear support player, the attacker taps the football into the teammate’s path.
When clean possession is unsafe and no teammate is available, the attacker may soccer the football towards the scoring gate or safer territory.
Play continues for five seconds after the initial action.
The defender applies controlled pressure.
One point is awarded for the correct action and one for a successful team outcome.
Rotate all roles after each repetition.
coachingPoints: Approach with the head and eyes up before lowering to the football.
Take clean possession whenever it can be done safely.
Tap only when a teammate is clearly positioned to receive.
Soccer the football with purpose rather than kicking blindly.
Avoid taking possession merely to be tackled immediately.
Protect the space between the defender and football.
Continue supporting after the initial action.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the player scans before reaching the football.
Whether clean possession is selected when available.
Whether taps are directed to a teammate’s advantage.
Whether soccer kicks create territory or simply surrender possession.
Whether players lower their eyes too early.
Whether support players communicate and remain active.

commonErrors.error: Player attempts to pick up every ground ball.
commonErrors.correction: Vary the closing pressure and score the action choice separately.

commonErrors.error: Player soccers despite having time.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce that clean possession provides the greatest control when safe.

commonErrors.error: Tap is made without checking for support.
commonErrors.correction: Require the support player to call before the tap is used.

commonErrors.error: Soccer kick travels directly to an opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Coach a clear target gate or boundary-side territory.

commonErrors.error: Player slows before reaching the football.
commonErrors.correction: Encourage acceleration through the final two steps when possession is available.

progressions: Permit controlled tackling.
Add a second defender.
Add a second support player.
Change the scoring gate according to field position.
Continue into a live 3v2 transition.
regressions: Practise each action separately before adding choice.
successIndicators: Scan pressure and support while approaching.
Tap accurately when a teammate has an advantage.
Soccer purposefully when possession is unsafe.
Continue into the next phase after the initial action.
matchApplication: Ground balls often require an immediate choice rather than a perfect pickup. Players must balance possession, pressure and territory to prevent stoppages, avoid being tackled and keep the football moving to team advantage.

title: Fundamental Decisions Assessment
primarySkill: Application of fundamental decision-making principles
objective: Assess players’ ability to apply the fundamental decision-making behaviours developed through DM-011 to DM-019 in a continuous, variable training activity.
groundSize: Half ground divided into a defensive start zone, midfield decision zone and attacking finish zone.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the squad into two teams.
Create three connected zones.
The defensive start zone contains boundary, corridor and reset options.
The midfield zone contains changing numerical situations and potential switch opportunities.
The attacking zone contains marking targets and a scoring gate.
Coaches position spare footballs around the ground to create imperfect-possession restarts.
Use controlled pressure initially, increasing intensity as the activity develops.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with possession in the defensive start zone.
Players must choose between the boundary, corridor or reset according to the defensive shape.
On entering the midfield zone, the coach releases an additional player to create either an attacking advantage, even numbers or a temporary disadvantage.
The team must recognise whether to continue forward, switch sides or retain possession.
A marked possession in the attacking zone requires an immediate play-on, hold or set-disposal decision.
At selected moments, the coach introduces an imperfect football to create broken play.
The attacking team scores one point for each correct decision and three points for completing the possession with a goal or target entry.
The defending team scores two points for forcing a poor decision and three for a turnover that produces a successful counterattack.
After a turnover, teams immediately reverse direction.
Play in four-minute blocks with one-minute review periods.
Rotate starting positions so all players experience different field zones.
Complete at least four blocks before recording assessment outcomes.
coachingPoints: Scan forward, wide and behind the football before possession.
Select receiving shape according to pressure.
Release immediately when the next target is ready.
Secure and rebalance when the disposal lane is not yet clear.
Confirm communicated options visually.
Play on after a mark only when a genuine advantage exists.
Use the switch when the ball side is overloaded.
Reassess immediately after fumbles, smothers and deflections.
Judge the decision separately from the execution result.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players scan before receiving.
Whether they identify forward options without forcing play.
Whether receiving orientation matches the pressure source.
Whether release tempo suits target readiness.
Whether communication is visually confirmed.
Whether post-mark decisions create or preserve advantage.
Whether teams recognise overloaded and open sides.
Whether players recover mentally after errors.
Whether field position changes the selected risk.
Whether decision quality is maintained as fatigue increases.

commonErrors.error: Players revert to predetermined patterns.
commonErrors.correction: Change defensive positioning and starting numbers between repetitions.

commonErrors.error: Coaches judge only whether the disposal was completed.
commonErrors.correction: Record decision quality and execution quality as separate scores.

commonErrors.error: Players become overly conservative under assessment.
commonErrors.correction: Reward appropriate attacking decisions even when execution fails.

commonErrors.error: Scanning decreases as fatigue increases.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce the duration of blocks while maintaining decision complexity.

commonErrors.error: Teams fail to react after an error or turnover.
commonErrors.correction: Award transition points during the first five seconds after possession changes.

commonErrors.error: Players depend on coach instructions.
commonErrors.correction: Use review questions between blocks rather than directing every live action.

progressions: Increase defensive pressure to match intensity.
Remove marked channels and gates.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Require nominated players to provide on-field leadership calls.
Record individual decision profiles across several sessions.
Begin from stoppages, kick-ins and turnover situations.
regressions: Assess one zone at a time.
Reduce the number of changing variables.
Allow a brief freeze before selected decisions.
Use smaller teams and shorter playing blocks.
Provide a single coaching focus for each player.
successIndicators: Select body orientation according to pressure.
Match release tempo to the situation.
Recognise when to switch or reset.
Adjust risk to field position and numerical balance.
Explain the reasoning behind their decisions.
matchApplication: The assessment recreates the changing information players process across a complete phase of Australian football. It connects defensive exit choices, midfield numbers, switching play, post-mark decisions and broken-play recovery in a continuous environment where the correct option changes from moment to moment.
relatedDrills: DM-015 – Mark, Play On or Hold

title: Receive, Run Through or Roll Out
primarySkill: Selecting movement after receiving possession
objective: Teach players to decide whether to continue running through the receiving lane, roll away from pressure or stop and release immediately after taking possession.
groundSize: 18 × 25 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Position a feeder at one end.
Place a receiver 12 metres away.
Set a continuation gate behind the receiver.
Mark a curved roll-out gate to one side.
Position one short-release target near the receive point.
A defender begins behind, beside or in front of the receiver.
howTheDrillWorks:
The receiver scans the defender before leading.
The feeder disposes to the receiver.
If the defender trails, the receiver continues running through the forward gate.
If the defender closes from the front, the receiver rolls away through the side gate.
If the defender arrives from the side and removes both movement lanes, the receiver releases immediately to support.
The receiver completes the next disposal after exiting.
One point is awarded for the correct movement choice.
One point is awarded for clean execution.
Rotate all roles after each repetition.
coachingPoints: Scan the defender’s starting position and movement.
Receive at speed when the forward lane is safe.
Roll towards space, not merely away from contact.
Use the body to protect the football.
Release immediately when movement lanes are closed.
Keep the feet active during possession.
Prepare the disposal before completing the turn.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether scanning occurs before possession.
Whether the receiver maintains momentum when unpressured.
Whether the roll-out moves away from the defender.
Whether players stop unnecessarily.
Whether the quick-release option is used when required.
Whether the football remains secure.

commonErrors.error: Receiver stops after every possession.
commonErrors.correction: Deliver the football into the running path and reward continuation.

commonErrors.error: Player rolls towards another defender or boundary.
commonErrors.correction: Require a scan of the exit space before turning.

commonErrors.error: Receiver turns into frontal pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Close the body and use the short-release option.

commonErrors.error: Player releases despite having open ground.
commonErrors.correction: Encourage continuation through the gate.

commonErrors.error: Football is carried on the pressure side.
commonErrors.correction: Shift it to the protected side during the movement.

progressions: Permit controlled tackling.
Add a second pressure player.
Remove the marked gates.
Add multiple support targets.
Continue into live 2v2 play.
regressions: Tell the receiver where pressure begins.
Practise one movement option at a time.
matchApplication: Players receiving through half-back, midfield or around stoppage must decide instantly whether to maintain momentum, evade pressure or move the football before being tackled.

title: Inside Runner or Outside Runner
primarySkill: Selecting the most effective running support lane
objective: Teach supporting players to choose an inside or outside running lane that complements the ball carrier and creates the greatest attacking advantage.
groundSize: 25 × 35 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Use three attackers against two defenders.
One attacker begins as the ball carrier.
Two supporting runners begin behind and to either side.
Mark an inside gate near the corridor and an outside gate near the boundary.
Defenders vary their width and closing positions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier advances towards the defenders.
Supporting runners scan the defensive shape and each other.
One runner selects the inside lane and the other holds outside width.
If the defenders compress centrally, the outside runner becomes the preferred option.
If defenders spread wide, the inside runner attacks the central gap.
The ball carrier draws a defender before releasing.
Attackers attempt to exit through either gate.
Two points are awarded for using the lane that best exploits the defensive shape.
Defenders counterattack after turnover.
Rotate all positions.
coachingPoints: Runners must occupy different lanes.
Hold outside width when central defenders compress.
Attack the inside gap when defenders separate.
Time the run so the ball carrier can draw pressure first.
Avoid crossing directly in front of another runner.
Communicate the selected lane.
Maintain defensive balance behind the play.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether runners select complementary lanes.
Whether the defensive shape is recognised.
Whether the preferred option changes correctly.
Whether runs begin too early.
Whether the ball carrier commits a defender.
Whether width and depth are maintained.

commonErrors.error: Both runners use the same lane.
commonErrors.correction: Allocate initial inside and outside roles, then allow live swapping.

commonErrors.error: Outside runner drifts towards the football.
commonErrors.correction: Mark a minimum-width channel.

commonErrors.error: Inside runner enters a congested corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Require a scan of defender spacing before accelerating.

commonErrors.error: Ball carrier releases before drawing pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Set a release line that must be reached first.

commonErrors.error: Runners cross and block one another.
commonErrors.correction: Use staggered depth and clearer communication.

progressions: Add a third defender.
Remove the marked gates.
Add a trailing support player.
Continue through a second phase.
Increase contact to match intensity.
successIndicators: Select the lane offering the strongest advantage.
matchApplication: Inside and outside runners help teams move through defensive lines. Their value depends on reading defender spacing and creating complementary rather than duplicated movement.

title: Late Runner Recognition
primarySkill: Recognising and using late-arriving support
objective: Teach players to identify late-arriving runners who enter space after defenders have committed to earlier options.
groundSize: 25 × 35 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one ball carrier at the starting end.
Place two early targets inside the area with two defenders.
Position one late runner behind the ball carrier.
Mark a central arrival zone and two wider target zones.
The late runner may enter only after the first two targets begin moving.
howTheDrillWorks:
The early targets lead and attempt to draw defenders.
The ball carrier scans their movement and defensive reaction.
The late runner delays, then accelerates into the space created behind or between defenders.
The ball carrier may use an early target if that player gains a clear advantage.
If defenders commit to the early movement, the late runner becomes the preferred option.
The receiver continues through one additional disposal or shot.
Two points are awarded for correctly using the late runner.
One point is awarded for correctly using an open early target.
Rotate all roles after each passage.
coachingPoints: Late movement must remain patient until defenders commit.
Accelerate sharply when the space opens.
The ball carrier must continue scanning after the first options appear.
Early targets should clear or hold defenders.
Do not ignore an early option that is genuinely free.
Deliver into the late runner’s path.
Communicate the late movement without alerting defenders too early.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the late runner delays sufficiently.
Whether early targets influence defenders.
Whether the ball carrier stops scanning too soon.
Whether the late arrival attacks useful space.
Whether the disposal leads the runner.
Whether defenders pass runners between them.

commonErrors.error: Late runner moves at the same time as early targets.
commonErrors.correction: Hold behind a release cone until defender commitment.

commonErrors.error: Ball carrier decides before the late option appears.
commonErrors.correction: Require a final scan immediately before disposal.

commonErrors.error: Early targets stop and crowd the space.
commonErrors.correction: Continue leads through the target area.

commonErrors.error: Late runner enters behind a defender.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust the entry angle to remain visible.

commonErrors.error: Ball carrier ignores an open early option.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce that late options are not automatically superior.

progressions: Add another late runner.
Permit defenders to switch.
Remove target zones.
Begin with a moving ball carrier.
Continue into live forward-entry play.
successIndicators: Use the runner who gains the greatest advantage.
matchApplication: Late runners regularly become dangerous through the midfield and inside 50 because defenders have already committed to earlier leads, contests or ball-side movement.

title: Movement Chain Under Pressure
primarySkill: Maintaining coordinated movement across multiple possessions
objective: Develop players’ ability to make consecutive movement decisions while pressure, ball position and teammate roles change throughout a possession chain.
groundSize: 35 × 45 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use two teams of five to ten players.
Position a scoring gate at each end.
Begin one team in possession.
No player may remain stationary for more than three seconds unless holding width or defensive balance.
At least one attacker must remain behind the football.
Defenders apply controlled match-like pressure.
howTheDrillWorks:
The possession team attempts to move the football through at least five disposals before scoring.
After each disposal, players choose whether to lead, overlap, hold, clear, fold or rotate.
The ball carrier must assess available space, pressure and support.
Defenders attempt to disrupt movement and force players into duplicated lanes.
A team receives one point for every five-disposal chain completed with clear width and depth.
Reaching the scoring gate adds two points.
A turnover creates immediate transition towards the opposite gate.
The coach may introduce a second football restart if play becomes congested.
Complete repeated two-minute blocks.
Review one movement decision between blocks.
coachingPoints: Scan before every movement change.
Avoid repeating the same running pattern after each disposal.
Maintain separate lanes around possession.
Replace space vacated by teammates.
Keep support behind unstable possession.
Use late movement after defenders commit.
Transition immediately when possession changes.
Maintain decision quality under fatigue.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether movement decisions remain connected across phases.
Whether players crowd the ball side.
Whether width and depth are maintained.
Whether late or overlapping runners are recognised.
Whether players replace vacated positions.
Whether movement quality declines under fatigue.
Whether transition reactions are immediate.

commonErrors.error: Players make one movement and then stop.
commonErrors.correction: Require an immediate next-role decision after every disposal.

commonErrors.error: All support moves ahead of the football.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain one designated rear support player initially.

commonErrors.error: Players repeat identical leads.
commonErrors.correction: Encourage holds, clears and rotations based on the picture.

commonErrors.error: Possession becomes crowded in one channel.
commonErrors.correction: Reward switches and separate-lane movement.

commonErrors.error: Players react slowly after turnover.
commonErrors.correction: Score the first five seconds of transition separately.

progressions: Remove all structural rules.
Increase contact to full legal match intensity.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Begin from stoppages or kick-ins.
Use full-ground dimensions.
regressions: Require only three disposals before scoring.
successIndicators: Make purposeful movement after every disposal.
matchApplication: Successful Australian football movement requires a chain of connected decisions rather than one isolated run. Players must continually update their role as possession, pressure and field position change.

title: Decision-Making Movement Phase Assessment
primarySkill: Integrated movement decision making under match-like pressure
objective: Assess players’ ability to coordinate movement before, during and after possession across the complete Decision Making movement-development phase.
groundSize: Half to three-quarter ground divided into defensive exit, midfield movement and forward-entry zones.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the playing area into three connected zones.
The defensive zone contains boundary, corridor and reset exits.
The midfield zone requires coordinated support, overlap and lane selection.
The forward zone contains leading, holding, clearing and late-run opportunities.
Use two balanced teams.
Position spare footballs around the area for rapid restarts.
Assign coaches or player leaders to record movement decisions.
howTheDrillWorks:
One team begins with possession in the defensive zone.
Players organise support ahead of and behind the football.
On entering midfield, players choose between carrying, releasing, overlapping, folding or holding shape.
Forward players coordinate early leads, decoy movement, clearing runs and late arrivals.
The attacking team scores three points for a goal or successful target entry.
One additional point is awarded for each clearly correct movement decision identified by the assessor.
The defending team scores for turnovers and successful counterattacks.
On turnover, both teams immediately reorganise into attacking and defensive lanes.
Coaches restart from different zones to vary the movement problem.
Play in four-minute blocks with one-minute review periods.
Rotate players through defensive, midfield and forward roles.
Complete at least four blocks before final assessment.
coachingPoints: Scan before moving and before receiving.
Decide whether to lead, hold, clear, overlap, fold or rotate.
Maintain separate lanes around possession.
Keep at least one player connected behind the football.
Use decoy and late movement to manipulate defenders.
Select inside or outside lanes according to defensive shape.
Replace positions vacated by teammates.
React immediately after turnovers.
Assess movement decisions separately from execution errors.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether movement begins after scanning.
Whether leading patterns remain coordinated.
Whether players select safe receiving paths.
Whether overlaps create genuine advantage.
Whether support remains ahead and behind possession.
Whether decoy and late runs affect defenders.
Whether players rotate into vacated positions.
Whether teams retain width and depth.
Whether transition lanes are filled quickly.
Whether decision quality survives fatigue and pressure.

commonErrors.error: Players follow fixed running patterns regardless of the picture.
commonErrors.correction: Change defender positions and restart locations regularly.

commonErrors.error: Too many players move towards the football.
commonErrors.correction: Score width, depth and clearing movement.

commonErrors.error: Teams lose all support behind possession.
commonErrors.correction: Require one player to hold defensive balance.

commonErrors.error: Early leads remain in the space and block late runners.
commonErrors.correction: Continue through the zone and clear fully.

commonErrors.error: Players fail to replace vacated positions.
commonErrors.correction: Use brief freeze-and-question reviews between blocks.

commonErrors.error: Coaches judge only disposal outcomes.
commonErrors.correction: Record movement decision and execution as separate measures.

progressions: Remove all marked zones and gates.
Increase pressure to full match intensity.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Begin from stoppages, kick-ins and intercepted marks.
Require player leaders to organise movement.
Record individual results across repeated sessions.
regressions: Assess one zone at a time.
Allocate one movement focus to each line.
Pause after selected possessions for guided questioning.
successIndicators: Coordinate leads, holds and clearing runs.
Select effective inside and outside lanes.
Use decoy and late movement purposefully.
Explain how their movement created or protected team advantage.
matchApplication: The assessment recreates the connected movement demands of Australian football from defensive exit through midfield progression and forward entry. It evaluates whether players can adapt their positioning and running patterns to the live game picture rather than relying on predetermined movement.

title: Corridor Collapse Decision
primarySkill: Responding when central space closes
objective: Develop players’ ability to recognise when a planned corridor attack has closed and select whether to change angle, use width or retain possession.
groundSize: 30 × 35 metres divided into a central corridor and two outside channels.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a central corridor channel and two wider outside channels.
Use four attackers against three defenders.
Place a high-value scoring gate at the end of the corridor.
Place lower-value gates at the end of each outside channel.
Begin the ball carrier facing the corridor.
Defenders may leave the corridor open initially and then close it as possession develops.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with possession and assesses the corridor.
If central space is clearly available, attackers may move directly towards the corridor gate.
Defenders are permitted to collapse into the corridor after the first disposal.
The next ball carrier must recognise whether the central lane remains usable.
If the corridor closes, the team changes angle through an outside support player.
Attackers may later re-enter the corridor if defensive movement reopens it.
A successful corridor exit scores three points.
A wide exit followed by controlled retention scores one point.
A turnover in the corridor scores three points for the defenders.
Continue through the possession until an exit or turnover occurs.
coachingPoints: Reassess the corridor after every defender movement.
Do not continue with a planned central disposal when the lane has collapsed.
Move the football sideways or backwards to create a new angle.
Outside players must maintain width until needed.
Recognise when defensive collapse creates space on the opposite side.
Re-enter the corridor only when a genuine advantage reappears.
Keep support behind the football in case the attacking lane closes.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players reassess after the first disposal.
Whether the corridor is forced despite defensive collapse.
Whether outside players hold sufficient width.
Whether the ball is moved quickly enough to beat defensive recovery.
Whether the team recognises a reopened central lane.
Whether rear support remains available.
Whether turnovers produce immediate defensive transition.

commonErrors.error: Player follows the original corridor plan despite defenders closing it.
commonErrors.correction: Freeze the picture and ask what changed after the first disposal.

commonErrors.error: Wide players move centrally too early.
commonErrors.correction: Mark a minimum-width line they must hold until the switch begins.

commonErrors.error: Team abandons the corridor permanently after one closure.
commonErrors.correction: Encourage re-scanning for a later re-entry opportunity.

commonErrors.error: Ball carrier holds possession while the defence recovers.
commonErrors.correction: Use the nearest clear support option quickly.

commonErrors.error: Players kick across the corridor without checking interception risk.
commonErrors.correction: Require a visible passing lane and receiver advantage.

progressions: Remove channel markings.
Add a fourth defender.
Increase pressure to match intensity.
Introduce full transition after turnovers.
Add scoreboard scenarios rewarding either fast attack or controlled retention.
Begin from kick-ins or intercept marks.
regressions: Predetermine when the corridor will close.
Allow the coach to call the change of direction.
Use short kicks and handballs only.
successIndicators: Use width to change the defensive picture.
Re-enter the corridor when it becomes available.
matchApplication: Central ball movement can create rapid scoring opportunities, but the corridor may close while the football is travelling. Players must update the decision rather than continuing with a pattern that no longer matches the defensive shape.

title: Front-and-Centre Action Choice
primarySkill: Selecting the first action after front-and-centre possession
objective: Teach front-and-centre players to decide whether to take possession, release immediately, snap at goal, gain territory or protect the football after an aerial contest.
groundSize: A 25 × 30-metre area with goals or three target gates.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one attacker and one defender in an aerial contest.
Place one front-and-centre attacker and one defensive-side opponent at ground level.
Position one supporting attacker outside the contest.
Set goals or target gates ahead.
A kicker sends the football into the aerial contest.
Vary the contest location so the front-and-centre player experiences different field positions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The kicker sends a high football to the aerial contest.
The front-and-centre player times movement towards the likely drop zone.
If the football spills, the player scans pressure, goal location and support.
With time near goal, the player may take possession and snap or kick.
Under immediate pressure, the player may release to outside support.
If clean possession is unsafe, the player may knock or soccer the football towards team advantage.
The defensive-side opponent attempts to pressure or win the spill.
Two points are awarded for the correct first action.
A successful score or team exit adds one point.
Rotate all roles after several repetitions.
coachingPoints: Arrive at the contest moving rather than waiting underneath it.
Read the likely spoil direction.
Know the goal and boundary location before collecting.
Take clean possession when balance and time permit.
Use support when pressure arrives immediately.
Snap or kick only when the scoring opportunity is realistic.
Knock or soccer the football purposefully when possession is unsafe.
Continue after the first action.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Timing of the front-and-centre run.
Whether the likely drop zone is recognised.
Whether the player scans before taking possession.
Whether scoring attempts suit the available time and angle.
Whether support is used under pressure.
Whether emergency knocks or kicks create team advantage.
Whether defensive-side coverage is maintained.

commonErrors.error: Player stands beneath the aerial contest.
commonErrors.correction: Begin deeper and arrive as the football reaches the contest.

commonErrors.error: Player takes possession despite immediate frontal pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Use a quick release or controlled knock to support.

commonErrors.error: Player snaps at goal from a poor angle with teammates free.
commonErrors.correction: Scan goal, pressure and support before deciding.

commonErrors.error: Front-and-centre player overruns the drop zone.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust starting depth and arrival speed.

commonErrors.error: Outside support enters the contest and removes the release.
commonErrors.correction: Hold a clear passing angle outside congestion.

progressions: Add a second ground-level defender.
Use full legal aerial and ground-level pressure.
Remove marked starting positions.
Continue into live forward-50 play.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Vary the kick direction and spoil type.
regressions: Roll the football from the aerial contest.
successIndicators: Avoid low-percentage possession or scoring attempts.
matchApplication: Front-and-centre players can create scores or prevent defensive exits, but only when the first action matches the spill, pressure and field position. The best decision may be possession, release, territory or an immediate shot.

title: Pressure and Contest Phase Assessment
primarySkill: Integrated decision making through pressure and contested phases
objective: Assess players’ ability to gather information, select effective actions and maintain team structure across varied pressure, contest and transition situations.
groundSize: Half to three-quarter ground divided into four connected assessment zones.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Create four connected assessment zones:
Zone 1 – Contest and First Release: Begin with a stoppage, ground ball or aerial spill.
Zone 2 – Pressure Escape: Players respond to boundary pressure, a trap or a blocked disposal lane.
Zone 3 – Transition Choice: The possession team selects corridor, width or reset according to the defensive shape.
Zone 4 – Attacking Outcome: Players respond to an aerial contest, front-and-centre spill or turnover near goal.
Use two balanced teams. Position coaches or player leaders around the ground to record decision quality and execution separately.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins each passage with a contested football in Zone 1.
Players decide whether to possess, tap, protect or release.
The team winning possession attempts to exit through Zone 2.
Defenders apply one of several pressure problems, including a boundary trap, converging pressure or a smothered lane.
In Zone 3, attackers assess whether to use the corridor, switch wide or reset possession.
Zone 4 ends with a forward entry, aerial contest, front-and-centre opportunity or scoring attempt.
Each clearly correct decision scores one assessment point.
Successful execution scores a separate point.
A goal or completed target entry scores three team points.
A turnover followed by a successful counterattack scores three points for the opposition.
Coaches vary the starting contest and pressure problem on every passage.
Play in four-minute blocks with one-minute review periods.
Rotate players through inside, outside, defensive and attacking roles.
Complete at least five blocks before final assessment.
coachingPoints: Scan opponents, teammates, space and field position before possession.
Select possession only when it creates control.
Use support rather than attempting to escape every contest individually.
Recognise the boundary, corridor and turnover consequence.
Reassess when a disposal lane closes.
Maintain complementary ground-level roles around aerial contests.
Adapt stoppage exits when the planned side is pressured.
Spread only after possession becomes stable.
Keep support behind the football during transition.
React immediately to turnovers, spills and deflections.
Judge the decision separately from the execution result.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players scan before contests and receives.
Whether possession, knock and protection decisions suit the pressure.
Whether the first release moves away from congestion.
Whether players recognise boundary and corridor risks.
Whether traps and blocked lanes are identified early.
Whether aerial-contest ground-level roles remain balanced.
Whether stoppage exits adapt to the opposition shape.
Whether players spread at the correct time.
Whether transition maintains width, depth and rear support.
Whether teams counter-pressure immediately.
Whether decision quality is maintained under fatigue and contact.
Whether players can explain the reasoning behind their choices.

commonErrors.error: Players focus only on winning the initial contest.
commonErrors.correction: Score the first release and transition decision separately.

commonErrors.error: Ball winners attempt to escape without using support.
commonErrors.correction: Require visible lateral or rear options around the contest.

commonErrors.error: Players continue with the original plan after pressure changes.
commonErrors.correction: Use guided questions about what changed in the picture.

commonErrors.error: Too many teammates enter congestion.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce nearest, support and spread roles.

commonErrors.error: Teams attack the corridor regardless of defensive coverage.
commonErrors.correction: Reward correct wide or reset decisions.

commonErrors.error: Players stop following a spill, deflection or turnover.
commonErrors.correction: Continue scoring through the next phase of play.

commonErrors.error: Coaches assess only successful disposals.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain separate decision and execution scores.

progressions: Increase contact to full legal match intensity.
Remove all marked zones and gates.
Add scoreboard, time and field-position scenarios.
Begin from boundary throw-ins, kick-ins, centre bounces and intercepted marks.
Require player leaders to organise exits and transition.
Extend the activity to full-ground dimensions.
Record individual decision profiles across repeated sessions.
regressions: Assess one zone at a time.
Give each player one specific decision focus.
Use controlled football feeds rather than live contests.
successIndicators: Connect contest wins to organised transition.
Explain why their decisions suited the game picture.
matchApplication: This assessment connects the major pressure and contest problems players face in Australian football. It measures whether they can win or recover possession, escape pressure, reorganise support and transition into attack without losing awareness of turnover risk, field position or team structure.

title: Forward 50 Entry Method
primarySkill: Selecting the most effective forward 50 entry
objective: Develop players’ ability to choose between a leading target, deep contest, short possession or lateral entry according to forward structure and defender positioning.
groundSize: From the centre square to the goal line.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use six to twelve attackers against five to eleven defenders.
Position one or two leading forwards, one deeper target and at least two ground-level attackers.
Mark a lead-up zone, deep contest zone and lateral entry lane.
Begin possession 60–75 metres from goal.
Defenders vary whether they defend aggressively, zone space or protect the deepest target.
Require one attacking player to remain outside the immediate forward contest.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team gains possession outside forward 50.
The ball carrier scans all forward targets and the defensive shape.
If a forward has clear separation, the football is delivered into the lead.
If the deep target has aerial advantage and ground-level support, a deeper entry may be selected.
If central options are closed, attackers use lateral possession to improve the angle.
A short option may be used when it creates a better next entry rather than merely delaying.
A mark inside 50 scores two points.
A ground-level possession from a purposeful deep entry scores one point.
A goal scores three additional points.
Defenders counterattack immediately after turnover.
coachingPoints: Scan all forward options before choosing the entry.
Kick to the receiver’s advantage, not simply towards a player.
Use a deep contest only when aerial and ground-level structure support it.
Avoid bombing the football to an outnumbered target.
Change the angle when defenders protect the central lane.
Short possession should improve the next entry.
Forward players must coordinate leads, holds, clears and ground-level positioning.
Maintain defensive balance outside the contest.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the ball carrier scans multiple targets.
Whether the chosen entry matches forward advantage.
Whether disposals are placed into space.
Whether deep entries have ground-level support.
Whether forwards crowd the same lane.
Whether lateral possession improves the entry angle.
Whether attackers defend the turnover.
Whether players force entries under pressure.

commonErrors.error: Ball carrier kicks deep without assessing numbers.
commonErrors.correction: Require identification of aerial and ground-level advantage first.

commonErrors.error: Multiple forwards lead into the same space.
commonErrors.correction: Coordinate one lead, one hold and one clearing movement.

commonErrors.error: Entry is directed at the receiver’s body.
commonErrors.correction: Kick into the forward’s running path.

commonErrors.error: Team uses short possession without improving the picture.
commonErrors.correction: Change angle, draw a defender or create a new lead before the next entry.

commonErrors.error: Ground-level attackers stand beneath the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain front-and-centre, defensive-side and outside-release roles.

progressions: Remove target-zone markings.
Increase pressure to full match intensity.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Begin from turnovers and stoppage exits.
Require repeat entries after defensive rebounds.
Rotate players through forward and midfield roles.
regressions: Work on one entry method at a time.
successIndicators: Select an entry suited to numbers and positioning.
matchApplication: Forward entries must match the positions of forwards, defenders and supporting players. A long entry, lead-up kick or lateral possession is only effective when it creates or preserves a genuine scoring advantage.

title: Kick-or-Handball Chain Choice
primarySkill: Selecting disposal type within team ball movement
objective: Teach players to select whether a kick or handball best maintains advantage, protects possession and supports the next phase of team ball movement.
groundSize: 30 × 45 metres divided into short, medium and long disposal zones.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Use five to ten attackers against four to nine defenders.
Divide the field into three lengthwise zones.
Position short handball support around the ball carrier and longer kicking targets ahead.
Defenders vary whether they close the carrier, block the short release or protect the longer target.
Place a scoring gate at the far end.
No disposal type is compulsory.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with possession in the first zone.
The ball carrier scans pressure, support distance and the next receiving advantage.
A handball is selected when it releases a moving teammate or escapes immediate pressure.
A kick is selected when it accesses space, changes the angle or reaches a teammate beyond the defensive line.
Players must avoid handballing to a stationary teammate under equal pressure.
They must also avoid kicking when a short release would preserve greater advantage.
Reaching the final gate scores two points.
A bonus point is awarded when every disposal type in the chain is judged appropriate.
Defenders score for turnovers or forcing possession backwards.
Teams reverse direction after turnovers.
coachingPoints: Select disposal type from the picture, not personal preference.
Handball should release a teammate into space.
Kick when it accesses territory or a player beyond pressure.
Avoid handballing responsibility to a teammate in a worse position.
Avoid kicking over a clearly available running support player.
Match disposal speed and height to the target.
Re-scan immediately after receiving.
Maintain balance before executing either skill.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether disposal type suits distance and pressure.
Whether handballs release moving players.
Whether kicks access advantage beyond the defensive line.
Whether players repeatedly favour one disposal type.
Whether support targets remain visible.
Whether the selected skill allows continuation.
Whether execution remains controlled under pressure.

commonErrors.error: Player handballs to a stationary teammate under pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Use a moving support option or protect possession.

commonErrors.error: Player kicks despite a clear overlap runner.
commonErrors.correction: Recognise the short release that preserves numerical advantage.

commonErrors.error: Player uses handball over excessive distance.
commonErrors.correction: Select a kick when the target is beyond effective handball range.

commonErrors.error: Player kicks high to a teammate without aerial advantage.
commonErrors.correction: Use a lower, faster disposal or shorter option.

commonErrors.error: Players decide the disposal type before scanning.
commonErrors.correction: Require recognition of pressure and target movement first.

progressions: Add a second line of defenders.
Remove the zone markings.
Introduce scoreboard and time scenarios.
Increase pressure to match intensity.
Require a switch of disposal type after the defence adapts.
Extend the activity across half a ground.
regressions: Provide only one short and one long option.
Predetermine one defensive problem at a time.
successIndicators: Select disposal type from the live situation.
Use kick to access space or territory.
Avoid transferring pressure to a teammate.
Execute accurately at the required tempo.
matchApplication: Effective team ball movement depends on selecting the disposal that best suits pressure, distance and teammate movement. Neither kicking nor handballing is automatically superior; the value comes from the advantage created.

title: Kick-In Shape Decision
primarySkill: Selecting a kick-in method
objective: Teach players to select and execute an appropriate kick-in method according to the opposition press, teammate positioning and available continuation options.
groundSize: From the goal square to the centre square.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use a full defensive kick-in structure.
Position the opposition in varied presses:
High man-on-man.
Central zone.
Boundary-side press.
Loose full-ground zone.
Mark short pockets, central release areas, switch zones and long-kick contest zones.
Require the possession team to organise ground-level support around any long target.
Rotate the kick-in player regularly.
howTheDrillWorks:
The kick-in player scans the opposition press before bringing the football into play.
Teammates establish short, wide, central and long options.
Against an unguarded short option, the kicker may release quickly.
Against a boundary-side press, the team may switch through the opposite pocket or central release.
Against a high press, the team may use movement behind defenders or a structured long kick.
A kick-in exit beyond defensive 50 scores two points.
A clean exit that directly exploits the press scores an additional point.
A turnover inside defensive 50 gives the opposition three points.
Play continues until possession reaches midfield, a turnover occurs or the football leaves the area.
Change the press before each restart.
coachingPoints: Identify the press before deciding the kick-in method.
Short possession is useful only when the receiver has continuation.
Use movement to create separation rather than standing at fixed cones.
Maintain weak-side width.
Long kicks require aerial and ground-level structure.
Avoid kicking to a contest where the opposition has numerical advantage.
Use the full protected area where competition rules permit.
Communicate the selected exit shape quickly.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the kicker scans the complete setup.
Whether short options have a viable next disposal.
Whether player movement creates separation.
Whether weak-side width remains available.
Whether long targets have appropriate support.
Whether the exit method suits the press.
Whether players react after a turnover.
Whether the kicker delays until the press is fully set when an earlier option existed.

commonErrors.error: Kicker selects the preferred side before scanning.
commonErrors.correction: Require identification of the press before bringing the football into play.

commonErrors.error: Short receiver is trapped immediately.
commonErrors.correction: Ensure the receiver has a second option or space to play on.

commonErrors.error: Long kick goes to an outnumbered contest.
commonErrors.correction: Count aerial and ground-level numbers before disposal.

commonErrors.error: Weak-side players move towards the ball too early.
commonErrors.correction: Hold width until the kick-in direction is confirmed.

commonErrors.error: Teammates remain stationary.
commonErrors.correction: Use coordinated leads, rotations and clearing movement.

progressions: Remove marked zones.
Allow the opposition to change press during the kick-in.
Add scoreboard and time pressure.
Increase defensive pressure to match intensity.
Continue into full-ground transition.
Require player leaders to organise the setup without coach direction.
regressions: Tell the possession team which press will be used.
Use one kick-in method at a time.
Begin with a free short option.
Reduce the distance required for a successful exit.
successIndicators: Create short, long, central and switch options.
Exit defensive 50 without unnecessary turnover risk.
matchApplication: Kick-ins provide structured possession but are immediately challenged by organised defensive presses. Players must select the exit method that best matches the opposition shape rather than relying on one rehearsed pattern.

title: Clock Management Possession
primarySkill: Managing possession against the match clock
objective: Teach players to manage the remaining match time through controlled possession, territory, stoppages and selective attacking play.
groundSize: Half to full ground.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use two balanced teams.
Set a visible countdown clock between 30 seconds and three minutes.
Give one team a narrow lead.
Begin possession from defensive 50, the midfield or attacking 50.
Mark safe support zones, boundary targets and attacking gates during introductory repetitions.
Normal football rules apply unless modified by the coach.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach announces the score, time and possession location.
The leading team attempts to manage possession until the clock expires.
Players may retain possession, gain territory, use the boundary or create a controlled stoppage.
The trailing team applies pressure and attempts to force an immediate turnover.
The leading team may attack goal when a high-percentage opportunity appears.
A completed possession sequence that removes 20 seconds from the clock scores one point.
Reaching a safe forward territory zone scores one point.
A turnover in a dangerous position gives the trailing team an immediate scoring opportunity.
The scenario ends when time expires, a score occurs or possession changes twice.
Reverse roles and change the starting field position.
coachingPoints: Know how much time remains before every disposal.
Use safe possession without becoming stationary.
Move opponents to create uncontested options.
Use the boundary when it reduces turnover consequence and can create a stoppage.
Avoid kicking long to an outnumbered contest merely to gain distance.
Take a high-percentage scoring opportunity when it can secure the result.
Maintain wide, short and rear support.
Communicate when to hold, attack, use territory or create a stoppage.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players know the remaining time.
Whether possession remains purposeful.
Whether safe options are created through movement.
Whether the boundary is used intelligently.
Whether players kick to unnecessary contests.
Whether high-percentage scoring chances are recognised.
Whether communication is clear.
Whether turnovers occur in dangerous central positions.

commonErrors.error: Players hold possession without creating the next option.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain movement and rebuild support before pressure arrives.

commonErrors.error: Team kicks long to an outnumbered contest.
commonErrors.correction: Use short possession or safe territory when no aerial advantage exists.

commonErrors.error: Players refuse a clear scoring opportunity.
commonErrors.correction: Recognise when a score can effectively end the contest.

commonErrors.error: Boundary use traps a teammate without support.
commonErrors.correction: Provide an inside and rear release before using the line.

commonErrors.error: Players lose awareness of the clock.
commonErrors.correction: Require regular time calls from leaders and the bench.

progressions: Conceal the clock from some players.
Change the time during the passage.
Add limited interchanges or fatigue.
Begin from live turnovers.
Increase pressure to match intensity.
Require players to manage the scenario without coach calls.
successIndicators: Use territory and the boundary appropriately.
matchApplication: Late-game possession requires more than keeping the football. Teams must use the clock, field position and available scoring opportunities while avoiding turnovers that give the opposition a direct path to goal.
relatedDrills: DM-015 – Mark, Play On or Hold

title: Tactical Method Switch
primarySkill: Changing team method during play
objective: Develop players’ ability to recognise when the current team method is ineffective and collectively switch to an alternative ball-movement or defensive approach.
groundSize: Three-quarter to full ground.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use two balanced teams across three-quarter or full-ground space.
Assign each team several recognised methods, such as:
Fast corridor attack.
Controlled boundary possession.
Weak-side switch.
High defensive press.
Deeper defensive zone.
Begin with one nominated method.
The coach alters opposition positioning or field conditions to make the original method less effective.
Team leaders are responsible for identifying and communicating the required switch.
howTheDrillWorks:
Teams begin playing using the nominated tactical method.
The opposition adapts its structure to reduce the method’s effectiveness.
Players scan for repeated problems such as blocked corridors, overloaded boundaries or exposed defensive space.
A team leader calls a tactical change.
Players reorganise their width, depth, tempo and positional roles.
A successful method change that creates a scoring opportunity or defensive stop scores two points.
Continuing with an ineffective method and conceding a turnover gives the opposition one point.
The coach may change the tactical problem again during the passage.
Play continues through goals, turnovers and restarts.
Review the trigger and quality of each tactical switch between blocks.
coachingPoints: Recognise repeated patterns rather than reacting to one isolated error.
Identify whether the problem is space, numbers, pressure, tempo or positioning.
Communicate the tactical change with simple agreed language.
All lines must adjust together.
Do not switch methods so frequently that team structure becomes confused.
Maintain core principles such as support and defensive balance during the change.
Reassess whether the new method is improving the game picture.
Player leaders should explain the reason for the change.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players identify an ineffective pattern.
Whether the tactical trigger is accurate.
Whether leaders communicate clearly.
Whether defenders, midfielders and forwards adjust together.
Whether the new method addresses the actual problem.
Whether the team changes too late or too often.
Whether core support and turnover protection remain.
Whether players reassess after the switch.

commonErrors.error: Team persists with a method that is repeatedly blocked.
commonErrors.correction: Identify the repeated defensive response and select an alternative.

commonErrors.error: Only the ball-side players change their behaviour.
commonErrors.correction: Require all lines to adjust positioning and roles.

commonErrors.error: Tactical call is vague or misunderstood.
commonErrors.correction: Use short, agreed team terminology.

commonErrors.error: Team changes method after one execution error.
commonErrors.correction: Separate skill failure from a genuine tactical problem.

commonErrors.error: New method removes defensive balance.
commonErrors.correction: Retain support behind the football during the change.

progressions: Remove coach-created tactical problems and allow the opposition to adapt independently.
Conceal tactical calls from the opposition.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Increase pressure to full match intensity.
Allow captains to control all tactical changes.
Analyse the session through video after training.
successIndicators: Recognise when the current method is failing.
Identify the cause of the problem.
Improve the game picture through the change.
Avoid unnecessary or constant tactical switching.
matchApplication: Opposition tactics, weather, scoreboard conditions and player positioning can make an established method ineffective. Teams must recognise the problem and adjust collectively rather than waiting for formal breaks in play.

title: Team Tactical Decision Assessment
primarySkill: Integrated team tactical decision making
objective: Assess players’ ability to recognise and respond to changing team-level tactical problems across defensive exits, midfield possession, forward entries and match scenarios.
groundSize: Full ground preferred; three-quarter ground minimum.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Prepare a series of tactical scenarios covering:
Defensive kick-in against varied presses.
Possession against man-on-man, zone and hybrid defence.
Use of a spare defender.
Midfield tempo changes.
Repeat forward entries.
Last-line defensive disadvantage.
Narrow scoreboard margins.
Late-game clock management.
Assign player leaders for each line.
Coaches score decision quality separately from execution.
Use full rules with controlled contact appropriate to the group.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins with a tactical scenario card.
Teams play the scenario for two to four minutes.
Players must identify the opposition structure, scoreboard context and required team method.
Defensive passages may begin with a kick-in, intercept or last-line numerical disadvantage.
Midfield passages require tempo, width, corridor and support decisions.
Attacking passages require forward-entry and repeat-entry choices.
The coach may change the scoreboard, clock or opposition structure during play.
Team leaders may call tactical adjustments without stopping the activity.
One assessment point is awarded for each correct team-level decision.
Execution quality is scored separately.
Goals and successful defensive exits retain normal team value.
Teams reverse roles between scenarios.
Complete at least six different tactical situations.
Finish with a player-led review of the strongest and weakest tactical decisions.
coachingPoints: Identify the opposition structure before applying a team method.
Use the exposed space created by defensive concentration.
Adjust movement against direct, zonal and hybrid defence.
Position spare defenders according to danger rather than the football alone.
Select kick-in methods with clear continuation.
Reassess forward structure before repeat entries.
Protect the most dangerous space when defending outnumbered.
Change risk and tempo according to score and time.
Communicate tactical changes clearly across all lines.
Maintain width, depth, support and turnover protection throughout every adjustment.
Judge decision quality separately from execution.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players recognise defensive presses.
Whether attacking movement changes against different defensive methods.
Whether spare defenders protect dangerous space.
Whether kick-in choices suit the press.
Whether repeat forward entries are reassessed.
Whether last-line defenders delay and protect effectively.
Whether scoreboard margin changes the risk level.
Whether players manage possession against the clock.
Whether tactical method switches are timely and coordinated.
Whether leaders communicate clearly.
Whether width, depth and turnover protection remain.
Whether decisions remain effective under fatigue and match pressure.

commonErrors.error: Players use rehearsed patterns without reading the opposition.
commonErrors.correction: Require identification of the tactical problem before judging the method.

commonErrors.error: One line changes method while others continue the previous structure.
commonErrors.correction: Use clear line-leader communication and shared tactical calls.

commonErrors.error: Teams confuse execution errors with tactical failure.
commonErrors.correction: Assess whether the decision was correct before changing the method.

commonErrors.error: Players ignore score or time.
commonErrors.correction: Display both clearly and require regular leader calls.

commonErrors.error: Tactical changes remove width or defensive protection.
commonErrors.correction: Preserve core structural principles during every adjustment.

commonErrors.error: Coaches provide answers during live play.
commonErrors.correction: Use player-led decisions and review the reasoning between scenarios.

progressions: Remove coach-issued tactical cards and allow teams to create problems for one another.
Use full match intensity and competition rules.
Conceal the scoreboard from selected players.
Require captain-only tactical communication.
Add fatigue through repeated four-minute blocks.
Record and review video of tactical decisions.
Extend the activity into a complete practice match.
regressions: Assess one tactical problem at a time.
Allocate one tactical responsibility to each line.
successIndicators: Adjust movement against man-on-man, zone and hybrid defence.
Make productive kick-in and defensive-exit choices.
Communicate and execute tactical changes collectively.
Explain the reasoning behind tactical decisions.
matchApplication: Australian football requires teams to solve changing tactical problems without constant coach intervention. This assessment measures whether players can identify opposition methods, understand game context and coordinate an effective team response across all areas of the ground.

title: Deceptive First Option
primarySkill: Using deception before disposal
objective: Develop players’ ability to use their eyes, body position and movement to influence a defender before selecting and executing the most effective disposal.
groundSize: 18 × 25 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one ball carrier in the centre of the area.

Place three target players ahead, laterally and behind the ball carrier.

Position one defender between the ball carrier and the targets.

The defender is permitted to react to the ball carrier’s eyes, shoulders and early movement.

Each target occupies a separate passing lane.

A feeder begins the repetition by disposing to the central player.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The central player scans all three options before receiving.


2. The feeder delivers the football.
