3. The defender attempts to read and close the most likely disposal.


4. The ball carrier uses a look, shoulder turn, step or controlled ball movement to suggest one option.


5. When the defender shifts, the ball carrier selects the newly available target.


6. The deception must remain balanced and must not delay the disposal until pressure arrives.


7. One point is awarded for moving the defender.


8. A second point is awarded for selecting and hitting the correct target.


9. The defender scores one point for remaining balanced and forcing a poor disposal.


10. Rotate feeder, ball carrier, defender and target roles.
coachingPoints: Scan every genuine option before attempting deception.
Use deception to create advantage, not merely to appear skilful.
Keep the football protected and disposal-ready.
Move the defender with the eyes and shoulders before changing the target.
Avoid turning the entire body so far that the replacement option becomes difficult to execute.
Dispose as soon as the defender commits.
Recognise when the defender remains balanced and use the original best option.
Maintain stable feet through the final disposal.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the player scans all targets before receiving.
Whether the deceptive action influences the defender.
Whether balance and disposal technique are maintained.
Whether players attempt deception when a direct option is already clear.
Whether the replacement target has genuine advantage.
Whether the defender reacts to body and eye cues.
Whether disposal occurs before pressure closes.

commonErrors.error: Player performs deception without scanning the real options.Require the player to identify all targets before receiving.
commonErrors.correction: Deception is exaggerated and slows the disposal.Use a smaller eye, shoulder or foot movement.

commonErrors.error: Ball carrier exposes the football while faking.Keep the football close and on the protected side.
commonErrors.correction: Player predetermines the second option.Select the target according to the defender’s actual response.

progressions: Add a second defender protecting another lane.
Allow targets to move after the deceptive action.
Introduce controlled tackling pressure.
Remove the fixed target lanes.
Require the ball carrier to disguise a kick before using a handball or vice versa.
Continue into live 3v2 transition.
regressions: Predetermine which option the defender will close.
Allow the ball carrier to start in possession.
Walk through the deceptive movement before increasing speed.
successIndicators: Select the option created by the defender’s movement.
matchApplication: Elite players create space by manipulating defenders before disposal. A convincing look, body turn or step can open a handball lane, release a teammate or prevent an intercept without requiring additional physical space.

title: Look-Off and Release
primarySkill: Disguising the intended receiver
objective: Teach players to hold or redirect a defender’s attention before releasing the football to a receiver outside the defender’s immediate focus.
groundSize: 20 × 25 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one ball carrier in the centre.

Place four receivers around the outside of the area.

Position two defenders between the ball carrier and the receivers.

One defender protects the forward half and one protects the lateral or rear half.

Receivers may move within short target zones.

A feeder supplies the ball carrier from behind or from the side.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The ball carrier scans all four receivers before possession.


2. The feeder delivers the football.


3. Defenders track the ball carrier’s head, shoulders and football position.


4. The ball carrier looks towards one receiver long enough to hold or shift a defender.


5. Without losing balance, the player releases to another receiver whose lane has opened.


6. The receiver continues possession to a second target.


7. Two points are awarded when the look-off clearly creates the passing lane.


8. One point is awarded for a correct direct release when deception is unnecessary.


9. Defenders score for an intercept or for forcing the ball carrier to hold beyond three seconds.


10. Rotate all roles after several repetitions.
coachingPoints: Use peripheral vision to retain awareness of the intended target.
Look off the defender, not the teammate.
Keep the disposal action compact and repeatable.
Do not stare at the false option so long that the real target closes.
Recognise defenders who refuse to follow the eyes.
Use a direct disposal when the best lane is already open.
Receivers must continue moving and remain available.
Follow the disposal to provide the next support option.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the player scans before receiving.
Whether the defender’s attention is manipulated.
Whether the intended target remains visible peripherally.
Whether the disposal is accurate despite the player looking elsewhere.
Whether receivers maintain movement.
Whether players use deception unnecessarily.
Whether defenders learn to remain balanced.

commonErrors.error: Player loses awareness of the real target.Complete the full scan before beginning the look-off.
commonErrors.correction: Disposal becomes inaccurate because the player’s body faces away.Keep the hips and feet balanced towards the likely release area.

commonErrors.error: Look-off lasts too long.Release on the defender’s first clear shift.
commonErrors.correction: Player uses the same false target every repetition.Vary the look direction and intended receiver.

progressions: Permit defenders to intercept at full speed.
Add a third defender.
Remove the three-second possession limit but increase physical pressure.
Allow receivers to rotate positions during the play.
Require a disguised kick to one target and a disguised handball to another.
Continue into a live possession game.
regressions: Predetermine the false and real targets.
Allow the player to begin with possession.
successIndicators: Retain awareness of the intended target.
Release at the moment the lane opens.
Use direct options when deception is not required.
matchApplication: Looking off a defender can open central handball lanes, create forward entries and prevent opponents from leaving their direct opponent early. The action is most valuable when it changes the defender’s decision without delaying possession.

title: Dummy Lead Response
primarySkill: Recognising and using false attacking movement
objective: Develop players’ ability to recognise when an attacking lead is being used to move a defender and identify the genuine receiving option created by that movement.
groundSize: 25 × 35 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Position one ball carrier outside the attacking area.

Use three attacking players against three defenders.

Mark a central lead-up zone, a deep target zone and a lateral space.

One attacker is assigned to initiate the first movement, but the movement may become a real or dummy lead depending on the defender’s response.

The other attackers must respond to the space created.

The ball carrier is not told which player should receive.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The first attacker makes an aggressive lead into the central zone.


2. The direct defender decides whether to follow, hand over or hold space.


3. If the defender follows, a second attacker moves into the vacated space.


4. If the defender holds and the first attacker gains separation, the initial lead becomes the genuine option.


5. The third attacker maintains width or depth to prevent defensive compression.


6. The ball carrier scans the entire interaction and selects the player with the best advantage.


7. A correct use of the space created by the first lead scores two points.


8. A correct pass to the initial leader when left free scores one point.


9. Defenders score for forcing all attackers into the same area or intercepting the disposal.


10. Rotate attacking roles and starting positions.
coachingPoints: The first lead must be fast enough to demand a defensive response.
A dummy lead is determined by the defender’s reaction, not by a fixed instruction.
Secondary movement should occur after the defender commits.
Avoid entering the vacated space too early.
The ball carrier must scan beyond the first movement.
Maintain a third option to stretch the remaining defenders.
Use the initial leader when the defence refuses to follow.
Deliver into the receiver’s path.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the first movement influences the defender.
Whether secondary movement is timed after commitment.
Whether the ball carrier scans beyond the first option.
Whether the initial leader is used when free.
Whether attackers preserve separation.
Whether defenders communicate handovers.
Whether the disposal enters the created space.

commonErrors.error: The first lead is too slow to influence the defender.Require a match-speed acceleration through the lead-up zone.
commonErrors.correction: Secondary attacker moves before the defender commits.Delay until the defender clearly follows or holds.

commonErrors.error: Ball carrier assumes the first lead is always a decoy.Use the initial leader whenever the defender leaves that player free.
commonErrors.correction: All attackers move towards the same space.Maintain one wide or deep option throughout the action.

progressions: Allow defenders to switch opponents.
Add a fourth attacker and defender.
Remove target zones.
Begin with the ball carrier moving at speed.
Add a late midfielder entering the play.
Continue into a live scoring phase.
regressions: Use two attackers against one defender.
successIndicators: Select the attacker with genuine advantage.
matchApplication: Forward structures often use one movement to create another. Players must understand that the value of a lead may be the space it creates, while remaining ready to use the original leader when the defender does not respond.

title: Delayed Disposal Window
primarySkill: Holding possession until advantage develops
objective: Teach players to recognise when an immediate disposal would waste an emerging advantage and when delaying briefly will create a better release option.
groundSize: 20 × 30 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one ball carrier at the base of the area.

Place two supporting attackers ahead and one behind.

Position two defenders between the carrier and forward targets.

One supporting attacker begins moving immediately.

The second enters late from a delayed starting cone.

The defenders decide whether to press the carrier, hold the first target or track the late runner.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The ball carrier receives and scans the first available options.


2. The early support player presents immediately.


3. The late runner enters after a one- to two-second delay.


4. If the early target has clear advantage, the ball carrier releases immediately.


5. If defenders remain balanced and the late runner is likely to create the spare, the carrier protects possession briefly.


6. The ball carrier releases as soon as a defender commits or the delayed option enters advantage.


7. Holding beyond the useful window allows defenders to close all options.


8. Two points are awarded for a correctly timed delayed release.


9. One point is awarded for a correct immediate disposal.


10. Defenders score for trapping the carrier or forcing an ineffective delay.
coachingPoints: Delay only when a better option is actively developing.
Protect the football and remain balanced while waiting.
Do not hold possession simply because a late runner exists.
Release immediately when the first option already has advantage.
Watch defender commitment rather than counting a fixed number of seconds.
Use small foot movements to maintain space and disposal angle.
Support players must time movement precisely.
Avoid delaying until the disposal window closes.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the player distinguishes between useful and unnecessary delay.
Whether possession remains protected.
Whether defenders are manipulated by the hold.
Whether the late runner creates genuine advantage.
Whether immediate options are ignored.
Whether the final release occurs before pressure arrives.
Whether support movement is properly timed.

commonErrors.error: Ball carrier always waits for the late runner.Use the first option whenever it already has clear advantage.
commonErrors.correction: Player disposes immediately before the defence commits.Hold briefly when the developing movement can create a spare.

commonErrors.error: Delay becomes static possession.Maintain active feet and change the disposal angle.
commonErrors.correction: Player holds until tackled.Release on the defender’s first decisive commitment.

progressions: Add controlled tackling pressure.
Introduce two late runners from different directions.
Remove the delayed starting cone.
Allow defenders to disguise their intended commitment.
Add scoreboard consequences for turnovers.
Continue into a live 4v3 transition.
regressions: Predetermine whether the early or late option will be best.
Increase the starting distance of pressure.
successIndicators: Recognise when immediate disposal is best.
Hold possession only while advantage develops.
matchApplication: Some advantages appear only after a defender commits or a late runner arrives. Elite decision makers can hold possession briefly without becoming trapped, allowing the team’s movement to create a stronger option.

title: Third-Player Chain
primarySkill: Using a third player to bypass pressure
objective: Develop players’ ability to recognise when a direct disposal is covered and use a third teammate to connect possession around or through defensive pressure.
groundSize: 25 × 35 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Use four attackers against three defenders.

Position one initial ball carrier, one high target, one lateral connector and one runner behind the football.

Defenders protect the direct lane between the carrier and high target.

Mark an outside connector zone and a central continuation gate.

The third player may receive laterally, behind or through an angled lane.

Defenders may leave the direct option open on selected repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The ball carrier scans the direct target and support structure.


2. If the direct lane is clearly available, the player may use it.


3. If a defender blocks the direct lane, the carrier releases to the third-player connector.


4. As the connector receives, the original target and ball carrier reposition.


5. The connector uses a one-touch or controlled second disposal to access the runner released beyond pressure.


6. Attackers attempt to exit through the continuation gate.


7. Two points are awarded for a successful third-player connection that bypasses the defensive line.


8. One point is awarded for using the direct option when it is genuinely open.


9. Defenders score for disrupting the connector or forcing a backward trap.


10. Rotate all attacking and defensive roles.
coachingPoints: Recognise when the direct lane is covered.
The connector must create a different angle, not stand behind the same defender.
Move the football faster than defenders can adjust.
The final receiver should begin movement as the first release occurs.
Use one-touch disposal only when the target and lane are ready.
The original ball carrier must continue moving after release.
Avoid using the third player when the direct option already has advantage.
Maintain support behind possession.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the direct lane is correctly assessed.
Whether the connector creates a distinct angle.
Whether final movement begins at the right time.
Whether the chain is fast enough to beat defensive adjustment.
Whether one-touch disposal is used appropriately.
Whether the original ball carrier continues supporting.
Whether defenders recognise and close the connector.

commonErrors.error: Connector stands in the same defensive lane as the target.Move laterally or behind to create a new passing angle.
commonErrors.correction: Ball carrier uses the connector despite an open direct option.Take the simpler advantage when it is available.

commonErrors.error: Final runner moves before the first disposal and is tracked.Begin acceleration as the connector receives.
commonErrors.correction: Connector one-touches without confirming the target.Secure possession when the final lane is not yet clear.

progressions: Add a fourth defender.
Remove marked support zones.
Allow defenders to switch assignments.
Continue into a second third-player chain.
Increase contact to match intensity.
Extend the activity across half a ground.
regressions: Use three attackers against one defender.
matchApplication: Third-player connections allow teams to bypass direct pressure, move through a defensive line and release runners who cannot be accessed from the original possession angle.

title: Numerical Bait and Switch
primarySkill: Drawing defenders before transferring to the spare side
objective: Teach players to attract defensive numbers towards one area before transferring possession to a genuine spare player or open side.
groundSize: 40 × 50 metres divided into ball-side, corridor and weak-side channels.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use six to twelve attackers against five to eleven defenders.

Begin possession in one outside channel.

Position two or three attackers close enough to combine on the ball side.

Place at least two attackers on the weak side.

Defenders may remain balanced or compress towards repeated ball-side possession.

Mark a scoring gate at the end of each outside channel.

Require one attacker to remain behind possession as the switching outlet.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. Attackers begin with one or two controlled disposals on the ball side.


2. The team scans whether defenders are being drawn towards the repeated possession.


3. If defenders compress, the rear outlet receives and initiates the switch.


4. Weak-side players hold width until the football begins transferring.


5. The switch may travel through the corridor, a rear player or a two-player chain.


6. If defenders refuse to compress, attackers may continue through the original side.


7. A successful weak-side gate entry after drawing three or more defenders scores three points.


8. A successful ball-side entry against balanced defence scores one point.


9. An intercepted transfer scores two points for defenders.


10. Teams reverse direction after turnovers.
coachingPoints: Ball-side possession must be credible enough to attract defenders.
Do not hold or overuse the football once compression has occurred.
Scan the weak side before the transfer begins.
Keep the rear outlet at sufficient depth.
Weak-side players must preserve width.
Transfer quickly enough to beat defensive recovery.
Continue on the original side when defenders do not commit.
Maintain turnover protection during the switch.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether ball-side possession attracts defenders.
Whether players recognise the moment of compression.
Whether the rear outlet remains available.
Whether weak-side width is maintained.
Whether the transfer is safe and fast.
Whether teams switch without first moving the defence.
Whether the original side is used when still advantageous.
Whether intercept risk is assessed.

commonErrors.error: Team switches before defenders have compressed.Complete credible ball-side possession and reassess the numbers.
commonErrors.correction: Ball-side players continue combining after the spare side appears.Transfer immediately once the defensive shift creates advantage.

commonErrors.error: Weak-side players move towards the football.Hold position beyond the minimum-width line.
commonErrors.correction: Rear outlet is too flat and easily pressured.Create greater depth and a safer angle behind possession.

progressions: Remove channel markings.
Allow defenders to disguise their compression.
Add full transition after interception.
Require a switch through two different disposal types.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Extend across full-ground dimensions.
regressions: Begin with a clear weak-side numerical advantage.
Allow the coach to call the switch.
successIndicators: Exploit the spare side with controlled possession.
matchApplication: Teams can create space away from the football by attracting defenders through credible possession. The switch becomes valuable only after the opposition has committed enough numbers to create a genuine spare side.

title: Turnover Trap Recognition
primarySkill: Recognising deliberate defensive bait
objective: Develop players’ ability to recognise when an apparently open option is being deliberately offered by the defence to create an intercept or pressure trap.
groundSize: 35 × 45 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use six to twelve attackers against six to twelve defenders.

Position three potential receiving lanes: short, corridor and wide.

Defenders secretly nominate one lane as the trap.

In the trap lane, the immediate receiver appears open, but a second defender is positioned to close, intercept or tackle on possession.

Attackers maintain lateral and rear support options.

Place a scoring gate beyond each lane.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The attacking team begins with possession at one end.


2. Defenders shape the area so one target appears unusually open.


3. The ball carrier scans the receiver, the passing lane and nearby defenders.


4. If the option is genuine, the disposal may be used.


5. If a defender is positioned to close the receiver immediately or intercept the next action, the ball carrier rejects the bait.


6. Attackers move the defence through another option and may return to the lane later.


7. A successful exit through a genuine option scores two points.


8. Identifying and rejecting the trap scores one decision point.


9. A turnover in the nominated trap scores three points for defenders.


10. The defending team changes the trap lane after every passage.
coachingPoints: Assess what happens after the receiver takes possession.
An apparently free player may still be in a poor receiving position.
Scan defender depth and closing angle.
Identify interceptors sitting behind or beside the target.
Reject options that transfer immediate pressure without continuation.
Move the defence before returning to the previously trapped lane.
Support players should create alternative angles.
Maintain turnover protection behind the football.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether ball carriers assess beyond the first receiver.
Whether hidden or second-line defenders are recognised.
Whether players dispose to targets who are technically free but tactically trapped.
Whether alternative support is available.
Whether the rejected lane becomes usable later.
Whether defenders coordinate the trap.
Whether the team protects against turnover.

commonErrors.error: Player assumes every unmarked teammate is a good option.Assess pressure, field position and the receiver’s next action.
commonErrors.correction: Ball carrier watches only the immediate defender.Scan the second line and likely interceptor.

commonErrors.error: Attackers avoid the trapped lane for the rest of the passage.Move the defence and reassess whether the option later becomes genuine.
commonErrors.correction: Supporting players remain stationary.Create new angles when the first option is rejected.

progressions: Allow defenders to change the trap during possession.
Use multiple apparent bait options.
Remove marked lanes.
Increase pressure to match intensity.
Add scoreboard and field-position consequences.
Begin from kick-ins, forward entries and stoppage exits.
regressions: Tell attackers which lane may be trapped.
Mark the second defender’s starting zone.
successIndicators: Reassess the lane after moving the defence.
matchApplication: Defences often concede an option intentionally to direct possession towards pressure, an intercept defender or the boundary. Players must judge the complete next phase rather than simply disposing to the first unmarked teammate.

title: Consequence-Based Risk Game
primarySkill: Selecting risk according to consequence
objective: Develop players’ ability to adjust decision risk according to field position, likely reward, turnover consequence and current match context.
groundSize: Half to three-quarter ground divided into defensive, midfield and attacking zones.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the area into defensive, midfield and attacking zones.

Use two balanced teams.

Assign different scoring and turnover values to each zone:

Defensive-zone safe exit: two points.

Midfield line break: two points.

Attacking-zone high-value entry: three points.

Defensive-zone turnover: three points to the opposition.

Midfield turnover: two points.

Attacking-zone turnover: one point.


Prepare scenario cards that alter the score, time or required outcome.

Display the current values clearly.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. One team begins with possession in a nominated zone.


2. Players scan the available options and understand the consequence of failure.


3. They select a conservative, balanced or aggressive action according to the picture.


4. The coach may change the scoreboard or time during play.


5. The team scores according to the successful action completed.


6. The opposition receives the nominated turnover value when possession changes.


7. Players must not choose low risk automatically; higher-value options should be used when the probability and match need justify them.


8. Play continues through transitions so the risk context changes with field position.


9. Complete 90-second to two-minute blocks.


10. Review one high-risk and one low-risk decision after each block.
coachingPoints: Risk is determined by both probability and consequence.
The same disposal may be appropriate in attacking 50 and unacceptable in defensive 50.
Recognise when the scoreboard requires greater attacking risk.
Do not become overly conservative when a clear advantage exists.
Consider what the opposition will receive after a turnover.
Maintain support behind higher-risk attacks.
Communicate the team’s current risk level.
Reassess whenever field position, score or time changes.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players understand the consequence values.
Whether decisions change by field zone.
Whether teams become too conservative.
Whether high-risk actions are forced without advantage.
Whether scoreboard context changes behaviour.
Whether support protects the football behind aggressive play.
Whether players communicate the preferred risk level.
Whether reasoning matches the actual game picture.

commonErrors.error: Players always select the highest-value option.Consider the probability of success and turnover consequence.
commonErrors.correction: Team avoids all attacking risk.Reward correct high-value decisions when genuine advantage exists.

commonErrors.error: Players ignore field position.State the turnover outcome before each passage.
commonErrors.correction: Team increases risk without maintaining defensive protection.Keep support behind the football during aggressive attacks.

progressions: Hide the exact scoring values and require players to infer consequence.
Change score and time during a passage.
Remove the zone markings.
Increase pressure to full match intensity.
Allow captains to set the team’s risk level.
Use full-ground practice-match conditions.
regressions: Use one field zone at a time.
Reduce the number of scenario changes.
successIndicators: Identify likely reward and turnover consequence.
Explain the reasoning behind the decision.
matchApplication: Advanced decision making requires more than choosing an open teammate. Players must judge the likelihood and consequence of each action in relation to field position, score, time and team structure.

title: Multi-Phase Scenario Adaptation
primarySkill: Adapting decisions across changing match phases
objective: Develop players’ ability to update decisions as possession, field position, numerical balance, defensive structure and match context change across a continuous passage.
groundSize: Three-quarter to full ground.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams.

Use three-quarter or full-ground dimensions.

Prepare scenario cards that alter one or more variables:

Possession changes.

Numerical advantage or disadvantage.

Defensive press.

Scoreboard margin.

Remaining time.

Field-position restart.

Weather or disposal restriction.


Assign line leaders responsible for communicating changes.

Coaches hold spare footballs for immediate restarts.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. Play begins from a nominated match situation.


2. After 30–60 seconds, the coach introduces a new scenario without stopping play.


3. Examples include releasing an extra player, changing the score, directing a new defensive press or restarting with a turnover.


4. Players must identify what has changed and adapt their decisions.


5. The team in possession may need to alter tempo, width, risk or target selection.


6. The defending team may need to change pressure, coverage or last-line protection.


7. One point is awarded when a team recognises and responds correctly within ten seconds.


8. Normal scoring continues.


9. Poor adaptation that creates a turnover or score gives the opposition an additional point.


10. Complete four- to five-minute blocks with short player-led reviews.


11. Rotate line leaders and tactical responsibilities.


12. Use at least six different scenario changes during the activity.
coachingPoints: Continuously update the game picture.
Identify exactly what changed before altering the method.
Avoid abandoning effective structure because of one new variable.
Communicate score, time, numbers and press clearly.
Adjust tempo collectively.
Maintain core principles of width, depth, support and turnover protection.
Recognise when the change affects only one line and when the whole team must adjust.
Review whether the adaptation improved the situation.
Separate tactical misreading from execution error.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Speed of recognition after a scenario change.
Accuracy of the tactical response.
Whether leaders communicate clearly.
Whether different lines adjust together.
Whether unnecessary changes are made.
Whether core support and defensive balance remain.
Whether score and time influence risk.
Whether players adapt again when possession changes.
Whether fatigue reduces awareness.
Whether teams can explain the trigger for their response.

commonErrors.error: Players continue with the previous method despite changed conditions.Require leaders to identify and call the new variable immediately.
commonErrors.correction: Team changes everything when only one element requires adjustment.Preserve unaffected structures and modify the specific problem.

commonErrors.error: Different lines respond in conflicting ways.Use one clear tactical call and line-leader confirmation.
commonErrors.correction: Players confuse a skill error with a tactical problem.Review whether the original decision remained correct.

progressions: Introduce two changes at once.
Conceal some scenario information from selected players.
Allow the opposition to create tactical changes independently.
Increase pressure to full match intensity.
Remove coach communication and use only visual signals.
Record the activity for post-session review.
regressions: Stop play when introducing each scenario.
Use one variable change at a time.
Keep the same leaders throughout the session.
successIndicators: Adapt tempo, risk, width and structure.
Distinguish tactical problems from execution errors.
Explain why the adaptation was selected.
matchApplication: Match conditions change continuously through turnovers, scores, time, opposition adjustments and numerical situations. Elite teams update their decisions while play continues rather than waiting for coach intervention or formal breaks.

title: Elite Decision Application Assessment
primarySkill: Integrated elite decision making
objective: Assess players’ ability to manipulate opponents, recognise hidden tactical information and adapt decisions across complex, high-pressure match phases.
groundSize: Full ground preferred; three-quarter ground minimum.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams.

Use a full-ground or three-quarter-ground playing area.

Prepare scenario conditions involving:

Defensive bait and intercept traps.

Man-on-man, zone and hybrid structures.

Numerical advantage and disadvantage.

Weak-side space.

Scoreboard and clock pressure.

Delayed runners and third-player connections.

Turnovers and disrupted possession.


Assign line leaders and independent decision assessors.

Record decision quality separately from skill execution.

Use controlled match-like contact.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. Play begins from a coach-selected restart.


2. The defending team is given a hidden tactical instruction, such as offering a bait option, compressing one side or protecting a specific lane.


3. The attacking team must identify the structure through live play.


4. Ball carriers may use deception, delayed release or third-player connections to create advantage.


5. The coach introduces scoreboard, time or numerical changes during the passage.


6. Teams must adapt without stopping play.


7. One assessment point is awarded for each clearly correct high-level decision.


8. A second point is awarded when the skill execution succeeds.


9. A successful tactical manipulation that directly creates a score receives a bonus point.


10. A turnover caused by failing to recognise a defensive trap gives the opposition two bonus points.


11. Play in four- to five-minute blocks.


12. Change the hidden tactical instruction between blocks.


13. Rotate leaders and player roles.


14. Complete at least six assessment blocks.


15. Finish with a player-led review using examples of correct decisions, incorrect decisions and correct decisions with failed execution.
coachingPoints: Scan beyond the immediate option.
Recognise defenders who are offering bait rather than losing position.
Use deception only when it changes the defensive picture.
Delay possession only while advantage is developing.
Use third-player connections to bypass covered direct lanes.
Draw defensive numbers before switching.
Adjust risk to field position, score and time.
Communicate tactical changes quickly.
Maintain width, depth and support behind possession.
Reassess after every turnover, score, deflection and structural change.
Judge the decision before judging the outcome.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players scan the second defensive line.
Whether deceptive actions create genuine advantage.
Whether release timing suits developing support.
Whether direct and third-player options are correctly compared.
Whether weak-side switches occur after defensive commitment.
Whether bait options and traps are recognised.
Whether risk changes with field position and match context.
Whether teams adapt after tactical changes.
Whether line leaders communicate clearly.
Whether support and defensive balance remain intact.
Whether decision quality survives fatigue and pressure.
Whether players can distinguish decision failure from execution failure.

commonErrors.error: Players use deception without a tactical purpose.Require the action to influence a defender or open a lane.
commonErrors.correction: Ball carriers overhold possession while waiting for a perfect option.Release as soon as a clear advantage develops.

commonErrors.error: Players take the first apparent option without scanning the next defensive layer.Assess the receiver’s pressure and continuation before disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Team switches sides before attracting defensive commitment.Draw numbers to the ball side before transferring.

commonErrors.error: Players maintain the same risk level regardless of score or field position.Recalculate the likely reward and turnover consequence.
commonErrors.correction: Coaches assess only possession outcomes.Record decision quality and execution separately.

progressions: Use full legal match intensity.
Remove coach-provided scenario cards and allow teams to design defensive traps.
Conceal the score or time from selected players.
Require captain-only tactical communication.
Introduce fatigue through repeated high-intensity blocks.
Use video review to analyse scans, defensive manipulation and decision timing.
Extend the assessment into a complete practice match.
regressions: Assess one advanced concept at a time.
Reveal the defensive instruction before play.
successIndicators: Recognise defensive bait and hidden pressure.
Adapt to score, time and tactical changes.
Maintain team support and turnover protection.
Explain the reasoning behind advanced decisions.
matchApplication: Elite Australian football decision making requires players to interpret hidden defensive intentions, manipulate opponents and adjust to changing match conditions. This assessment measures whether those behaviours can be applied continuously under realistic pressure rather than only in isolated drills.

title: Information Priority Under Chaos
primarySkill: Prioritising relevant information in a chaotic game situation
objective: Develop players’ ability to identify the most important information and make an effective decision when several opponents, teammates, calls and movement options compete for their attention.
groundSize: 35 × 45 metres divided into three decision zones.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple information sources and player feedback
setup:
Divide the area into three connected zones.

Use six to twelve attackers against five to eleven defenders.

Position forward, lateral and rear targets around the ball carrier.

Assign supporting players to provide genuine pressure, switch and time calls.

Give the coach coloured markers that change gate value or indicate a temporary numerical condition.

Defenders may close different lanes after possession begins.

Not every verbal or visual cue should require action.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The attacking team begins with possession in the first zone.


2. The ball carrier scans pressure, teammates, defenders, field position and target gates.


3. Supporting players provide several calls, including useful, unnecessary and occasionally conflicting information.


4. The coach displays a cue that changes one part of the game picture.


5. The ball carrier must identify which information directly affects the immediate decision.


6. Players progress through the zones by selecting suitable disposals or carries.


7. One point is awarded for identifying and acting on the most relevant information.


8. A second point is awarded for successful execution.


9. Defenders score two points for forcing a decision based on irrelevant or misleading information.


10. Teams reverse direction after turnovers.
coachingPoints: Prioritise immediate pressure and legal disposal options first.
Consider field position and turnover consequence before lower-value information.
Communication assists the decision but does not replace visual confirmation.
Ignore calls that do not improve the possession.
Avoid attempting to process every detail equally.
Re-scan after each disposal because the priority may change.
Maintain balance and ball protection while gathering information.
Use simple team language for urgent information.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players recognise the most urgent information.
Whether pressure and field position are considered.
Whether players blindly follow loud communication.
Whether visual cues distract players from genuine options.
Whether decision speed remains effective.
Whether supporting communication is concise and useful.
Whether players update priorities after the football moves.

commonErrors.error: Player attempts to respond to every call.Identify the information that directly changes the immediate decision.
commonErrors.correction: Loud communication overrides the visual picture.Require the ball carrier to visually confirm the target and passing lane.

commonErrors.error: Player focuses on a coach cue while pressure arrives.Prioritise immediate opponent pressure before secondary instructions.
commonErrors.correction: Players stop moving while processing information.Maintain active feet and body balance.

progressions: Add another defender and supporting target.
Introduce two simultaneous coach cues.
Conceal the scoring value of some gates.
Increase pressure to match intensity.
Add scoreboard and time information.
Continue into full-ground play without marked zones.
regressions: Use one communication source at a time.
Display only one clear visual cue.
successIndicators: Prioritise immediate pressure and field position.
Update priorities as the play changes.
matchApplication: Players process numerous voices, opponents, teammates and tactical cues during every possession. High-level decision makers identify which information matters immediately instead of becoming delayed or distracted by everything occurring around them.

title: Leadership Call and Player Override
primarySkill: Responding intelligently to tactical leadership calls
objective: Teach players to follow clear leadership calls when they suit the game picture while retaining responsibility to override or modify the call when immediate information makes it unsafe or ineffective.
groundSize: Half to three-quarter ground.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of leadership, tactical scenarios and player-led review
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams.

Nominate a captain and one line leader for each team.

Establish several simple calls, such as:

Switch.

Control.

Fast.

Boundary.

Corridor.

Hold.


Begin each passage from a different field position.

The opposition may change its shape after the leadership call.

Leaders cannot cancel or modify the call after the ball carrier begins the action.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. A team begins with possession.


2. The captain or line leader makes a tactical call.


3. Players begin reorganising according to the call.


4. The opposition then adjusts its shape or pressure.


5. Ball carriers and nearby players must determine whether the original call remains appropriate.


6. When the call remains suitable, the team executes it collectively.


7. When immediate pressure makes it unsafe, the ball carrier may override or modify the action.


8. Two points are awarded for correctly executing a suitable leadership call.


9. Two points are also awarded for a justified override that preserves or improves possession.


10. An unjustified override or blind obedience that causes a turnover gives the opposition two points.


11. Review the reasoning between passages.


12. Rotate leadership roles regularly.
coachingPoints: Leadership calls provide a shared method, not an excuse to ignore live information.
Players should follow the call unless a clear immediate reason prevents it.
Overrides must be based on pressure, lane closure, numbers or field position.
Communicate the override quickly so teammates can adjust.
Avoid changing the method because of personal preference.
Leaders should make early, simple and specific calls.
Players remain accountable for the final action.
Review whether the call or execution caused the outcome.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether leadership calls are early and clear.
Whether players reorganise collectively.
Whether the live game picture is visually confirmed.
Whether overrides are justified.
Whether players ignore calls without a clear reason.
Whether players follow instructions into obvious pressure.
Whether the team adjusts quickly after an override.
Whether leaders accept and review player decisions.

commonErrors.error: Player follows a call into a closed lane.Confirm the current pressure and passing lane before execution.
commonErrors.correction: Player ignores the call because another option is preferred.Override only when the original method is genuinely unsafe or unavailable.

commonErrors.error: Override occurs without teammate communication.Use a clear call such as “hold”, “change” or “reset”.
commonErrors.correction: Leader makes the call after possession is already pressured.Communicate before the ball carrier must act.

progressions: Conceal the opposition adjustment from team leaders.
Require captain-only tactical calls.
Change score and time during passages.
Increase pressure to full match intensity.
Use full-ground practice-match conditions.
Record leadership and override decisions for video review.
regressions: Tell players when an override will be required.
Allow coaches to support the leader.
successIndicators: Confirm the call against live information.
Override only for clear tactical reasons.
Accept responsibility for the final decision.
matchApplication: Players must respond to captains, line leaders and team calls while still reading the immediate game picture. Effective teams combine collective tactical direction with individual responsibility at the moment of action.

title: Attacking Mismatch Recognition
primarySkill: Identifying and exploiting an attacking mismatch
objective: Develop players’ ability to recognise a favourable size, speed, aerial or positional mismatch and create an appropriate opportunity without forcing possession.
groundSize: From the centre square to the goal line.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of tactical match-ups and forward structure
setup:
Use six to twelve attackers against six to twelve defenders.

Create several different match-up types:

Faster attacker against a slower defender.

Stronger aerial attacker against a smaller defender.

Mobile attacker against a less agile defender.

Defender positioned on the wrong side.


Do not announce the mismatch to the attacking team.

Position supporting forwards around the target area.

Begin possession 60–80 metres from goal.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The attacking team gains possession outside forward 50.


2. Players scan match-ups and positioning ahead.


3. When a favourable mismatch is identified, nearby attackers clear or hold defenders away from the target space.


4. The ball carrier chooses a disposal suited to the advantage:

Into running space for speed.

High and protected for aerial advantage.

Low and direct for positional separation.



5. If the defence provides support or removes the mismatch, attackers select another option.


6. A possession created from correctly identifying the mismatch scores two points.


7. A goal from the mismatch scores three additional points.


8. A forced entry after the defence has neutralised the advantage scores no decision point.


9. Defenders counterattack after turnovers.


10. Rotate match-ups and starting positions.
coachingPoints: Recognise the specific advantage rather than only the player’s identity.
Match the disposal type to the mismatch.
Clear space around the favourable contest.
Avoid bringing additional defenders towards the target.
Use the mismatch quickly before the defence reorganises.
Do not force the football when support has removed the advantage.
Maintain ground-level and turnover structure.
Communicate the mismatch without making the movement predictable.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players identify the correct mismatch.
Whether the disposal suits the type of advantage.
Whether teammates clear or crowd the target area.
Whether the ball is delivered before defensive support arrives.
Whether players force the same target after the mismatch is neutralised.
Whether ground-level support remains.
Whether the team protects the turnover.

commonErrors.error: Ball carrier identifies the player but not the type of advantage.Decide whether the mismatch is based on speed, strength, height or position.
commonErrors.correction: Disposal does not suit the mismatch.Kick into space for speed and protect aerial advantage with placement.

commonErrors.error: Supporting forwards lead into the isolation space.Clear away or hold defenders outside the target area.
commonErrors.correction: Team repeatedly targets the mismatch after defensive support arrives.Reassess whether the advantage still exists.

progressions: Allow defenders to switch match-ups.
Add a loose defender.
Remove marked isolation zones.
Begin from live turnovers.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Require players to identify mismatches across different field lines.
regressions: Tell attackers which match-up has an advantage.
Work with one mismatch type at a time.
successIndicators: Use the advantage before defensive support arrives.
Abandon the option when the mismatch is neutralised.
matchApplication: Teams can generate scoring opportunities by recognising favourable match-ups before the opposition has time to switch or provide support. The disposal and surrounding movement must suit the specific advantage.

title: Defensive Mismatch Protection
primarySkill: Protecting an unfavourable defensive match-up
objective: Teach defenders to recognise an unfavourable match-up and decide whether to switch, provide help, protect space or increase pressure on the ball carrier.
groundSize: Defensive half of the ground.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of defensive match-ups, communication and transition
setup:
Use six to twelve attackers against six to twelve defenders.

Create an unfavourable defensive match-up inside forward 50.

Position one potential help defender and one last-line defender nearby.

Begin the attacking possession 50–70 metres from goal.

Vary whether pressure can be applied to the ball carrier.

Defenders are not told in advance whether switching, helping or holding shape will be best.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The attacking team gains possession outside forward 50.


2. Defenders scan match-ups and identify the primary danger.


3. The direct defender communicates whether help or a switch is needed.


4. If a safe handover is available, defenders may switch opponents.


5. If switching would release another dangerous target, a help defender protects the likely disposal space.


6. When help positioning leaves another option exposed, teammates increase pressure on the ball carrier.


7. Defenders score one point for preventing the mismatch from receiving cleanly.


8. Winning possession and exiting defensive 50 scores two additional points.


9. Attackers score three points for a goal created through the mismatch.


10. Rotate match-ups and help-defender roles.
coachingPoints: Identify the most dangerous mismatch early.
Communicate before the forward movement begins.
Switch only when responsibilities are clearly transferred.
Help from a position that still allows recovery.
Increase pressure on the ball carrier when defensive coverage is vulnerable.
Avoid sending multiple defenders to the same opponent.
Maintain last-line protection.
Rebound with control after winning possession.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether defenders identify the mismatch.
Whether communication occurs early.
Whether switches are completed safely.
Whether help defenders protect the likely space.
Whether another dangerous attacker is released.
Whether pressure on the ball carrier improves.
Whether last-line protection remains.
Whether rebound decisions are controlled.

commonErrors.error: Defenders recognise the mismatch but do not communicate.Use an early, specific call identifying the opponent and required help.
commonErrors.correction: Help defender commits fully and leaves another attacker free.Position to influence the mismatch while retaining recovery ability.

commonErrors.error: Two defenders switch without confirming responsibilities.Complete a clear verbal and visual handover.
commonErrors.correction: Defenders focus only on the target and allow an unpressured entry.Increase pressure on the ball carrier to reduce disposal quality.

progressions: Allow attackers to rotate and create new mismatches.
Remove designated help defenders.
Increase pressure to match intensity.
Begin from turnovers and repeat entries.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Require player leaders to organise all defensive adjustments.
regressions: Predetermine whether to switch or help.
Reduce the number of attacking targets.
successIndicators: Maintain coverage of other dangerous options.
Apply pressure to the ball carrier.
matchApplication: Defensive match-ups change through rotations, injuries, transition and opposition tactics. Teams must recognise when help or switching is required without creating a larger problem elsewhere.

title: Weather-Adjusted Decision Game
primarySkill: Adjusting decisions to weather and ground conditions
objective: Develop players’ ability to adjust disposal type, possession method, field positioning and risk according to wind, rain, slippery ground or reduced visibility.
groundSize: Half to three-quarter ground.
equipment: Water spray for footballs where safe
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching with strong safety management
setup:
Use two balanced teams.

Prepare safe scenario conditions representing:

Strong wind towards one end.

Crosswind.

Wet or slippery football.

Slower ground movement.

Reduced marking reliability.


Do not create unsafe footing or uncontrolled wet surfaces.

Mark territory gates, short-possession zones and ground-level support areas.

Begin from varied field positions.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The coach announces or introduces the current weather condition.


2. Teams play towards the scoring end under normal football rules.


3. Players adjust disposal type, target location and possession method.


4. Into strong wind, teams may use lower disposals, shorter connections and running support.


5. With the wind, players judge carry distance and avoid overkicking targets.


6. In slippery conditions, players anticipate spills and increase ground-level support.


7. A decision suited to the condition scores one point.


8. Successful execution scores a separate point.


9. Unsafe or unrealistic disposal choices give the opposition one point.


10. Change the condition every three to four minutes.
coachingPoints: Adjust the decision before blaming execution.
Keep kicks lower and more direct into strong wind.
Allow for extra carry with the wind.
Use wider safety margins in a crosswind.
Expect marks and pickups to spill in wet conditions.
Maintain additional ground-level support.
Use territory when clean possession is difficult.
Avoid high-risk central disposals when conditions reduce control.
Protect player safety on slippery ground.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether disposal choices change with conditions.
Whether players adjust kick height and direction.
Whether ground-level support increases.
Whether players continue attempting dry-weather skills in slippery conditions.
Whether territory is used intelligently.
Whether central turnover risk is understood.
Whether players communicate wind and ground information.
Whether movement remains safe.

commonErrors.error: Players use the same disposal method in every condition.Identify how wind or moisture changes flight, bounce and control.
commonErrors.correction: High kicks are used into strong wind.Use lower, more penetrating disposals and running support.

commonErrors.error: Players stand for marks in wet conditions without ground support.Position teammates front and centre and defensive side.
commonErrors.correction: With-wind kicks travel beyond the target.Reduce force and allow for additional carry.

progressions: Change conditions without announcing them.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Increase pressure to match intensity.
Use opposing conditions in each half.
Allow player leaders to establish the method.
Continue into a full practice match.
regressions: Work with one condition at a time.
successIndicators: Adjust disposal height, distance and direction.
matchApplication: Weather and ground conditions change the probability and consequence of decisions. Successful teams adapt their method rather than attempting to play identical football regardless of wind, rain or surface quality.

title: Fatigue Decision Integrity
primarySkill: Maintaining decision quality under fatigue
objective: Develop players’ ability to preserve scanning, option selection and team structure as physical fatigue increases.
groundSize: 40 × 50 metres with two scoring gates.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of load, safety and decision assessment
setup:
Use two teams of six to twelve players.

Position a scoring gate at each end.

Play repeated high-intensity blocks of 60–90 seconds.

Provide short recovery periods.

Require at least one forward, one lateral and one rear support option.

Record decision quality during the first and final 20 seconds of each block.

Adjust work-to-rest ratios for age, fitness and playing level.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. Teams play continuously towards opposite scoring gates.


2. The coach begins with a contested or transition restart.


3. Players attempt to maintain scanning and support structure throughout the block.


4. A correct decision scores one assessment point.


5. Successful execution scores a separate point.


6. A rushed disposal, missed scan or structural collapse is recorded.


7. At the whistle, players recover briefly and receive one coaching question.


8. Repeat for four to six blocks.


9. Compare early-block and late-block decision quality.


10. Reduce workload immediately if technique or player safety deteriorates excessively.
coachingPoints: Continue scanning when breathing and movement become difficult.
Use simple, high-percentage options when skill control reduces.
Avoid confusing fatigue with urgency.
Maintain support behind the football.
Communicate clearly and early.
Reset mentally after errors.
Use body balance before disposal.
Recognise when the team needs controlled possession to recover structure.
Protect decision quality rather than chasing maximum physical output.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether scanning decreases late in blocks.
Whether players rush disposal.
Whether support becomes flat or disappears.
Whether communication reduces.
Whether players force high-risk actions.
Whether errors cause further poor decisions.
Whether physical load remains appropriate.
Whether decision quality improves across repeated blocks.

commonErrors.error: Players stop scanning when fatigued.Use a visible head-check requirement before receiving.
commonErrors.correction: Disposal becomes rushed and unbalanced.Secure body position before selecting the action.

commonErrors.error: Team loses rear support.Nominate and communicate one connected player behind possession.
commonErrors.correction: Fatigued players attempt increasingly difficult options.Use simpler possession until control and structure improve.

progressions: Increase block length gradually.
Reduce recovery periods.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Begin each block from a different match phase.
Increase pressure to full match intensity.
Track individual decision accuracy under fatigue.
regressions: Limit the number of consecutive repetitions for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Select options suited to declining control.
Limit the decline in decision quality.
matchApplication: Many decisive moments occur late in quarters and matches when players are fatigued. Teams that preserve scanning, structure and risk control are less likely to concede damaging turnovers.

title: Umpire Call and Advantage Decision
primarySkill: Responding correctly to umpire decisions and advantage opportunities
objective: Teach players to recognise umpire calls, determine whether advantage exists and either continue play or stop and use the free kick appropriately.
groundSize: 30 × 40 metres with a scoring gate at each end.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced management of whistle timing, legal interpretation and player discipline
setup:
Use two teams of five to eleven players.

Position a scoring gate at each end.

The coach acts as umpire.

During live possession, the coach calls free kicks, play on, touched, not 15 or advantage situations.

Some free kicks should provide a genuine continuation advantage.

Others should require the team to stop and use protected possession.

Players must not anticipate or dispute calls.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. Teams play continuously towards opposite gates.


2. The coach makes realistic umpiring calls during play.


3. When a free kick is called, players assess whether possession has continued to clear team advantage.


4. If advantage exists, the team continues without hesitation.


5. If advantage does not exist, the player stops and returns the football to the free-kick recipient.


6. When “play on” or “not 15” is called, the ball carrier must respond immediately.


7. One point is awarded for the correct advantage or stop decision.


8. Reaching the scoring gate scores two additional points.


9. Continuing after a call without advantage gives the opposition one point.


10. Undisciplined reactions or failure to return the football also score for the opposition.
coachingPoints: Listen while continuing to scan the play.
Advantage must be immediate, clear and beneficial.
Do not continue merely because the football remains with the team.
Use protected possession when the free kick provides a better outcome.
Respond instantly to play-on calls.
Avoid stopping when genuine advantage exists.
Return the football promptly and maintain discipline.
Teammates should communicate whether play remains advantageous.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players hear and understand the call.
Whether advantage is correctly assessed.
Whether teams continue into pressure unnecessarily.
Whether genuine advantage is lost through hesitation.
Whether players respond to play-on calls.
Whether teammates communicate.
Whether discipline is maintained after decisions.
Whether field position influences the choice.

commonErrors.error: Player continues because the team still has possession.Advantage must improve the team’s position, not merely preserve the football.
commonErrors.correction: Players stop despite a clear scoring opportunity.Continue immediately when the next action has genuine advantage.

commonErrors.error: Ball carrier ignores a play-on call.Respond with immediate movement or disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Players argue or delay returning the football.Reinforce discipline and immediate compliance.

progressions: Increase the speed and complexity of calls.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Use full match intensity.
Allow player umpires to control selected blocks.
Include 50-metre penalty consequences for indiscipline.
Extend into a full-ground practice match.
regressions: Explain each call before resuming play.
Use one call type at a time.
Display a coloured card with the verbal call.
successIndicators: Stop when protected possession is better.
matchApplication: Players lose opportunities and concede turnovers when they misread advantage, fail to hear play-on calls or react emotionally to decisions. Correct responses protect possession and preserve scoring opportunities.
relatedDrills: DM-015 – Mark, Play On or Hold

title: Final Two-Minute Scenario Chain
primarySkill: Managing connected decisions during the final two minutes
objective: Develop players’ ability to connect possession, territory, scoring and defensive decisions during the final two minutes of a close match.
groundSize: Three-quarter to full ground.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenario management, tactical assessment and player-led review
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams.

Prepare two-minute scenarios including:

Leading by one to five points with possession.

Leading by one to five points without possession.

Trailing by one to five points in defensive 50.

Trailing by one to five points inside attacking 50.

Scores level with possession in midfield.


Display the score and countdown clock.

Nominate captains and line leaders.

Begin from kick-ins, stoppages, marks or live turnovers.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. The coach announces the score, time and starting situation.


2. Teams play continuously for two minutes.


3. Players must manage possession and field position according to the scenario.


4. Teams protecting a lead may use controlled possession, safe territory and boundary stoppages.


5. Teams chasing the game must increase forward intent without abandoning turnover protection.


6. Teams with scores level must judge whether to attack, protect or create the final scoring opportunity.


7. Normal scoring applies.


8. One decision point is awarded for each action suited to the scenario.


9. Poor game-management decisions give the opposition one assessment point.


10. The scenario ends when time expires.


11. Reverse roles and begin a different field-position problem.


12. Complete four to six scenarios.
coachingPoints: Know the score, time, possession and field position.
The required risk can change after every disposal.
Protecting a lead still requires movement and useful territory.
Chasing the game requires urgency without blind forward disposal.
Use the boundary when a stoppage helps the team.
Avoid boundary play when the team urgently needs a score and central space is available.
Maintain defensive protection behind attacking play.
Communicate time regularly.
Recognise when a behind, stoppage or possession sequence is strategically valuable.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players know the score and time.
Whether decisions suit the current margin.
Whether teams manage territory effectively.
Whether possession becomes static.
Whether players force scoring attempts.
Whether defensive balance remains.
Whether captains communicate clearly.
Whether the method changes after scores and turnovers.
Whether players understand the value of stoppages.

commonErrors.error: Players forget the score or time.Require regular leader calls and visible scoreboard reference.
commonErrors.correction: Team leading becomes completely defensive.Maintain productive possession and a credible scoring threat.

commonErrors.error: Team trailing kicks blindly forward.Create the best available entry rather than surrendering possession.
commonErrors.correction: All players move ahead when chasing the match.Retain enough defensive protection to prevent an easy counterattack.

progressions: Hide the clock from selected players.
Change the score during the scenario.
Begin with fatigue from a previous high-intensity block.
Increase contact to full legal match intensity.
Limit tactical communication to player leaders.
Review decisions using video.
regressions: Use a visible clock and regular coach time calls.
Provide the team’s tactical objective before play.
matchApplication: Close matches are determined by connected decisions rather than one isolated moment. Players must continuously adjust to score, time, field position and possession across the final two minutes.
relatedDrills: DM-097 – Umpire Call and Advantage Decision

title: Unscripted Chaos Match
primarySkill: Adapting to unpredictable match events without coach direction
objective: Develop players’ ability to independently solve unpredictable game problems while maintaining team structure, communication and decision quality.
groundSize: Full ground preferred; three-quarter ground minimum.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenario design with minimal live intervention
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams.

Use normal positional structures.

Prepare hidden event cards including:

Sudden numerical advantage or disadvantage.

Change of defensive press.

Strong wind direction.

Scoreboard change.

Umpire-call sequence.

Injured-player simulation requiring positional rotation.

Wet-football period.

Reduced time remaining.

Opposition tactical switch.


Assign captains and line leaders.

Coaches introduce events without prescribing the response.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. Teams begin a normal practice match.


2. Every two to four minutes, the coach introduces an unscripted event.


3. Players must identify what changed and determine the response.


4. Captains and line leaders communicate any tactical adjustment.


5. Coaches do not provide the solution during live play.


6. One assessment point is awarded when a team recognises the event and responds effectively.

title: Decision Making Chapter Final Assessment
primarySkill: Complete application of Australian football decision making
objective: Assess players’ ability to gather information, select effective actions, coordinate team behaviour and adapt to changing match situations across the complete Decision Making chapter.
groundSize: Full ground preferred; three-quarter ground acceptable.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of full-ground assessment, tactical scenarios, load and feedback
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams.

Use full-ground positions and normal match structure.

Prepare assessment phases covering:

Pre-possession scanning.

Space and pressure recognition.

Numerical advantage.

Defensive exits.

Midfield tempo.

Forward entries.

Contested and broken play.

Turnovers and transition.

Team tactical adjustment.

Scoreboard and clock scenarios.

Leadership and player-led adaptation.


Assign coaches or trained observers to different ground areas.

Record decision quality separately from execution.

Use controlled contact suitable to the playing group.
howTheDrillWorks:
1. Begin with a normal match restart.


2. Allow an initial five-minute period of uninterrupted play to establish natural decision behaviour.


3. Introduce a defensive-press scenario through a kick-in or defensive possession.


4. Begin the next passage from a stoppage or contested football.


5. Introduce a numerical advantage or disadvantage during transition.


6. Change the defensive structure between man-on-man, zone and hybrid methods.


7. Include a forward-entry and repeat-entry phase.


8. Introduce a broken-play situation through a deflection, smother or imperfect football.


9. Change the score and remaining time for a final-match scenario.


10. Introduce one unexpected event requiring player-led adaptation.


11. Award one assessment point for each correct decision.


12. Award a separate point for successful execution.


13. Record team-structure decisions including width, depth, support and turnover protection.


14. Play in five-minute blocks with brief player-led reviews.


15. Rotate players through defensive, midfield and forward roles.


16. Complete at least six assessment blocks.


17. Finish with individual and team feedback based on recurring patterns rather than isolated outcomes.
